glossary.definition: The tendency of observers to explain others’ behavior by their dispositions while underweighting the situational pressures acting on them; also called correspondence bias.
Changing one’s judgments or behavior to match those of a group. In Asch-type tasks it is robust but varies with majority size, culture and era.
Repeating a study’s procedure as closely as possible with new participants to test whether the original result is reliable.
A replication whose protocol and analysis are fixed and reviewed in advance, often run across many laboratories, so that results are published regardless of outcome.
The claim that self-control draws on a limited resource used up by earlier acts of self-control; a large preregistered multi-lab test found an effect near zero.
A theory of motivation distinguishing autonomous from controlled motivation and proposing that support for autonomy, competence and relatedness fosters the former.
Doing an activity because it is interesting or satisfying in itself, rather than for a separable outcome such as pay or approval.
The process by which an externally prompted behavior comes to be valued and self-endorsed (identified or integrated regulation), making it autonomous though not intrinsically enjoyable.
When an external incentive weakens an existing intrinsic or social motive, for example by turning a moral obligation into a purchasable service; the reverse is crowding in.
The difficulty that arises when a principal delegates work to an agent whose actions cannot be fully observed and whose interests differ, creating hidden action and hidden information.

When an agent divides effort among tasks that differ in measurability, strong incentives on the measured tasks divert effort from the unmeasured ones; weaker incentives or job redesign may be optimal.
The heuristic that a measure loses its value as an indicator once it becomes a target, because people find cheaper ways to move the measure than the goal. Related to Campbell’s law.
How incentive pay changes with the measure — linear, threshold, capped, relative or deferred — which determines where marginal incentives are strongest and which gaming strategies pay.
Responding to kind actions with kindness and to unkind actions with retaliation, even at personal cost; it helps enforce incomplete contracts and norms.
Contributing to shared efforts when others do and withdrawing when others free ride, which makes group cooperation fragile without sanctions.
A shared expectation about what people do and ought to do, enforced informally through approval and disapproval.
The benchmark — prior outcome, peer outcome or expectation — against which an outcome is judged as a gain, a loss, fair or unfair.
A shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks such as asking questions or admitting errors; associated with learning and performance, mostly in correlational studies.

exercise.title: Incentive Designer

intro.text: You are the newly appointed director of patient-care operations at Linden Ferry Medical Center, a fictional mid-sized hospital. Unit 5 West, a 30-bed medical-surgical unit, has three problems leadership wants fixed: late-day discharges that back up the emergency department, a rising rate of patient falls, and mediocre patient-experience scores. The board has approved a modest incentive budget. Your job is to design the incentive system.

Choose one option on each of six dimensions: what is measured, whose performance counts, the time horizon, the payout shape, how performance is monitored, and which non-financial levers you use. The engine totals each option’s effects on six indicators and fires warnings for risky combinations. Try at least three designs: one that maximizes effort on the measured work, one that minimizes gaming, and one you would actually defend to the unit’s nurses. Notice which indicators move together and which trade off.

Every effect is an ordinal teaching heuristic grounded in this week’s readings, shown in words, not a prediction of what would happen in a real hospital. Open “Show the rules” at any time to see every number.

brief.text: Unit 5 West (fictional): 30 beds; about 60 nursing staff across shifts, plus nursing assistants, a unit clerk and a nurse manager. Discharges are often delayed by pharmacy, transport and physician sign-off, not only by nursing. Falls are rare events, so monthly counts are noisy. Patient-experience surveys have low response rates. Staff turnover is moderate, and a neighboring hospital is recruiting. Many nurses describe their motivation in terms of patient care and professional pride. All details are synthetic.

dimensions.label: What is rewarded
dimensions.help: The proxy that pay or recognition is attached to.

options.label: Share of discharges completed before noon
options.why: A precise, easily moved measure; part of it depends on other departments, and the cheapest ways to move it include discharging patients before they are ready or delaying admissions paperwork.

options.label: Patient-experience survey score
options.why: Valued by patients, but low response rates make it noisy, and staff can influence who is surveyed and how questions are framed.

options.label: Audited composite: timely discharge, falls, readmissions and chart quality
options.why: Covering several tasks reduces effort diversion predicted by the multitask model, at the cost of complexity and audit expense.

options.label: No formula: nurse manager’s structured judgment
options.why: Judgment can weigh unmeasured work, but it is open to favoritism and perceived unfairness unless criteria are explicit.

dimensions.label: Whose performance counts
dimensions.help: Individual, team, a mix, or rank among peers.

options.label: Individual nurse
options.why: Sharpens individual effort on attributable tasks, but discharges and fall prevention are team products; individual pay discourages helping.

options.label: Whole unit
options.why: Rewards cooperation and shared work; conditional cooperators may withdraw if free riding is visible and unaddressed.

options.label: Mostly unit, small individual component
options.why: Balances shared outcomes with some individual accountability; more complex to explain.

options.label: Ranking nurses against each other (top quartile paid)
options.why: Tournaments raise effort but turn colleagues into rivals; incentives read as distrust can erode reciprocity.

dimensions.label: Time horizon
dimensions.help: How often performance is measured and paid.

options.label: Monthly
options.why: Frequent feedback, but rare events like falls are mostly noise at monthly scale, and short horizons reward quick fixes.

options.label: Quarterly
options.why: A common compromise between feedback and noise.

options.label: Annual, with part deferred
options.why: Longer horizons average out noise and reduce timing games, but weaken the link between effort and reward.

dimensions.label: Payout shape
dimensions.help: How pay changes as the measure changes.

options.label: Linear: pay per point of improvement
options.why: Constant marginal incentive everywhere; highest power and cost.

options.label: Threshold: fixed bonus only if target met
options.why: Strong incentive only near the target; invites shifting results across periods and giving up when the target is out of reach.

options.label: Linear up to a cap
options.why: Limits extreme behavior and cost, but removes incentives above the cap.

options.label: No cash: recognition and resources only
options.why: Avoids pricing professional norms; weaker direct effect on volume tasks.

options.label: Unit self-reports its numbers
options.why: Signals trust and costs little, but makes cheap manipulation of the measure easy.

options.label: Random audits of a sample of records
options.why: Raises the cost of gaming without signalling blanket distrust.

options.label: Continuous electronic tracking of individual activity
options.why: Reduces some gaming but signals distrust and can crowd out reciprocity and professional pride.

options.label: Manager judgment informed by peer review
options.why: Uses local knowledge of unmeasured work; vulnerable to bias without clear criteria.

options.label: None
options.why: Leaves the social economy as it is.

options.label: Public leaderboard of individual scores
options.why: Adds status competition to the measured task; can feel controlling.

options.label: Peer-nominated recognition for safety catches and help
options.why: Informational recognition supports competence and relatedness and rewards hard-to-measure behavior.

options.label: Unit-led improvement projects with protected time
options.why: Supports autonomy and competence; costs staff time.

rules.text: Monthly pay on before-noon discharges is the classic recipe for discharging patients early or reclassifying discharge times. Watch readmissions and the timestamp process.
A ranking plus a public leaderboard makes colleagues rivals twice over. Expect less help across shifts and possible hoarding of easy patients.
Self-reported survey administration lets the unit choose which patients are surveyed. The score may rise without any change in care.
Monthly thresholds invite moving results across the month boundary and giving up mid-month when the target looks lost.
Team pay without any check on contributions relies entirely on peers to sanction free riding. Conditional cooperators may withdraw if a few people visibly coast.
Protected time for unit-led projects signals autonomy; continuous tracking signals distrust. Staff will notice the mixed message.
Judgment-based reward can capture unmeasured work, but only if criteria are published and decisions explained; otherwise fairness concerns will dominate.
A broad, audited measure over a long horizon is close to what the multitask model recommends for complex jobs. The price is weaker short-term effort and higher administration.
With no cash and no non-financial levers, this design changes little. That may be the right answer if the current problem is mostly caused by other departments.

config.disclaimer: Effects are ordinal teaching heuristics drawn from the cited research, not predictions of behavior in any real hospital. Linden Ferry Medical Center and all details are fictional.

debrief.text: Most learners discover three trade-offs. First, effort on the measured work and gaming risk tend to rise together: the stronger the incentive on a proxy, the more attractive cheap ways of moving it become. Second, individual and ranking schemes raise measured effort at the expense of cooperation, which matters in a unit where discharges and fall prevention are team products. Third, heavy monitoring reduces gaming but can damage intrinsic motivation and reciprocity; audits reduce gaming with less signal of distrust.

There is no best design. A unit-level, audited composite over a longer horizon, combined with recognition for safety catches, scores well on gaming and cooperation but weakly on immediate effort and costs more to administer. Whether that is right depends on facts the exercise cannot show: how much of the discharge delay is under nursing control, how staff interpret incentives, and how the neighboring hospital is recruiting.

What the exercise does not show: actual magnitudes, interactions beyond the listed rules, selection effects (who joins or leaves under each design), or how the design would be implemented and explained. Those questions are where executive judgment, piloting and measurement come in.

assumptions: Effects are ordinal (−3 to +3 per option) and simply add; real effects interact in many more ways than the listed rules capture.
Each option’s effect is a teaching heuristic drawn from the cited literature, not an estimate from hospital data.
Discharge timing depends partly on other departments; the unit cannot fully control it.
Falls are rare events, so short-horizon fall counts are dominated by noise.
Linden Ferry Medical Center, Unit 5 West and all details are fictional.

case.title: The Activation Accelerator
case.fiction: All people, organizations and data in this case are fictional. Lanternfish Payments is an invented company; any resemblance to a real firm is coincidental.

body.text: At 7:40 on a Tuesday morning, Nadia Ferreira-Holt, chief operating officer of Lanternfish Payments, opened a message from the company’s chief risk officer with the subject line “Need 30 minutes before the board deck goes out.” Lanternfish sold a bundle of payments, payroll and expense cards to small businesses — restaurants, contractors, clinics, independent retailers. It had grown quickly for six years, and in ten weeks it would ask investors for its largest funding round yet. The draft board deck, already circulating, led with a single chart: new-account activations up 61 percent in two quarters.

The chart was the product of the Activation Accelerator, a program Nadia had approved nine months earlier. Lanternfish’s account executives had always been paid a salary plus a commission on signed contracts. The problem, as the sales leadership saw it, was that many signed businesses never actually used the product. A customer who signed but never ran a payroll or swiped a card generated no revenue and usually left within a year. So the Accelerator shifted pay. Commission on signatures was halved; in its place, account executives received a bonus of $400 for each new account that “activated” within 30 days of signing. Activation was defined, for simplicity, as the first successful card transaction of any amount or the first payroll run.

The design had been debated. Mateo Varga, vice president of sales, had argued for it forcefully: “We are paying people to sign customers who never use us. Pay them for the thing that predicts revenue.” Theo Brandt, the chief financial officer, liked that the bonus was tied to a behavioral event rather than a promise. A data scientist on Theo’s team had shown that, historically, accounts that activated within 30 days were far more likely to still be active a year later. Nobody had asked whether that relationship would hold once people were paid on it.
What the numbers say

The early results looked excellent. Activations rose sharply, and the share of signed accounts that activated within 30 days climbed from about half to more than four in five. The sales team’s morale was high; several account executives earned the largest bonuses in the company’s history. Mateo had been invited to speak about the program at an industry conference.

The message from Ines Calloway, the chief risk officer, described a different picture. Her team had been reviewing first transactions for a fraud-model update and had noticed clusters. Across the last two quarters, 214 new accounts had activated with a single transaction of exactly $1.00. In 37 of them, the transaction originated from devices or networks associated with Lanternfish’s own offices. Nineteen of those 37 accounts belonged to the portfolio of one account executive, a top performer named Corey Lindqvist. The remainder were spread across eleven people. Ines had not yet spoken to anyone in sales.

There was more, and it was less clear-cut. Ninety-day retention of new accounts — the share still transacting three months after signing — had fallen from 58 percent to 46 percent over the same period, even as 30-day activation soared. Customer-support tickets from new accounts complaining about features they “did not know they had signed up for” had roughly doubled. A product manager suggested an innocent explanation for part of this: the Accelerator had brought in a wave of smaller businesses that churn more anyway. Nobody had yet separated the two effects.
The people in the room

Nadia called the four executives together that afternoon. Ines spoke first. “At minimum we have a control failure. At worst we have employees making transactions on customers’ accounts without authorization, which is a regulatory problem, not a sales problem. I want the bonus suspended today, the 37 accounts investigated, and a clawback on any bonus paid for an activation we cannot verify.”

Mateo pushed back. “Thirty-seven accounts out of thousands. Nineteen are one person. I am not going to tell 140 account executives they are under suspicion because of one bad actor and a few people who probably helped a customer test a card in the office — which, by the way, we used to encourage. If we suspend the bonus ten weeks before the raise, half my top performers will be interviewing at competitors by Friday. The program works. Retention is down because we are signing smaller customers, which is the strategy.”

Theo was quieter. He was worried about the board deck. The activation chart was the strongest evidence that Lanternfish’s growth was real rather than purchased. If the company disclosed that the metric was compromised, investors would discount every other number in the deck. If it did not, and the story emerged later, the damage would be worse. “I need to know,” he said, “whether the activation numbers are mostly real with some noise, or mostly noise with some real. I don’t think anyone in this room knows.”

Nadia also had a conversation she had not shared. A week earlier, a senior account executive with a long, clean record had told her privately that the team had a phrase — “a dollar to launch” — and that new hires learned it in their first month. He had not said whether he did it. He had said he was tired of being compared on a leaderboard with people who did.
What Nadia does not know

Nadia did not know how many of the 214 $1.00 activations were legitimate customer tests, how many were employees helping customers in good faith, and how many were employees activating accounts without customer knowledge. She did not know whether the fall in retention reflected gaming, a shift in the customer mix, or both. She did not know whether a public suspension would lead to resignations or whether most of the sales team would quietly welcome a clean reset. And she did not know whether the original data scientist’s finding — that early activation predicts retention — had ever reflected a causal relationship, or whether it simply identified customers who already intended to use the product.

She did know three things. The board deck would go to directors in six days. Any decision she made would be read by 140 account executives as a statement about whether the company trusted them. And whatever replaced the Accelerator would also be gamed by somebody, somehow, unless it was designed with that in mind.

At 6:15 that evening she opened a blank document and typed the heading: “Activation Accelerator — decision and redesign.” Then she stopped, because she was not sure whether the first section should be about the program, the people or the board.

exhibits.note: Synthetic data. Assumptions: quarters are labelled relative to launch; the customer mix shifted toward smaller businesses after launch, by an amount not yet measured.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 2 — First-transaction review by the risk team (last two quarters)
rows: …of which originated from Lanternfish office devices or networks
…of those 37, in one account executive’s portfolio
…of those 37, spread across other account executives
exhibits.note: Synthetic data. Assumptions: the review covered first transactions only; customer intent behind each $1.00 transaction is unknown.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 3 — Account-executive pay structure
rows: Activation bonus (first transaction or payroll within 30 days)
exhibits.note: Synthetic data. Assumptions: no clawback provision existed; activation was not verified beyond the system event.

assumptions: Lanternfish operates in a regulated industry where unauthorized transactions on customer accounts may create legal exposure; this case does not assess any legal question.
The historical correlation between early activation and retention was measured before anyone was paid on activation.
The customer mix shifted toward smaller businesses after launch, but the size of that shift has not been measured.
All figures are synthetic and chosen for teaching.
questions: Using the multitask model and Kerr’s diagnostic question, explain how the Accelerator’s design made a $1.00 activation an attractive strategy. Which features of the pay structure mattered most?

What should Nadia do in the next six days about the board deck, the 37 accounts and the bonus? Defend a position that a skeptical board member and a skeptical account executive could both accept as fair.
How would you separate the effect of gaming from the effect of the shifting customer mix on 90-day retention? What data would you need, and what would change your recommendation?
Design a replacement incentive. What is measured, over what horizon, with what payout shape and verification? What new form of gaming should Nadia expect, and how will she detect it?
What signals — about trust, fairness and the company’s norms — will 140 account executives read into each option, and how should that shape the way the decision is communicated?

perspectives.title: Suspend now, investigate, claw back
perspectives.text: The integrity of a financial metric and possible unauthorized activity on customer accounts outweigh short-term sales disruption. Suspend the activation bonus immediately, investigate the 37 accounts with risk and legal involvement, disclose to the board that the metric is under review, and introduce clawbacks for unverified activations. The cost is morale and possibly some departures; the benefit is that the company’s numbers, and its account executives, can be trusted again. This view treats the board deck as secondary to getting the facts right.

perspectives.title: Targeted investigation, redesign without public suspension
perspectives.text: Most activations are probably real, and a blanket suspension tells honest employees they are suspects. Investigate the 37 accounts and the individual with 19 of them quietly and promptly; change the definition of activation going forward (for example, a minimum transaction value, multiple transactions or a payroll run, verified as customer-initiated); remove the leaderboard; disclose to the board that the metric is being tightened and why. The risk is that the problem is wider than it looks and the company is later seen to have moved too slowly.

perspectives.title: Replace the measure, not just the rules
perspectives.text: The core mistake was paying on a single early event because it historically correlated with retention. Any single-event activation measure will decay under pay pressure. Replace the activation bonus with a smaller, deferred bonus based on 90- or 180-day revenue from the account, with team-level components to reduce rivalry, and present the board with retention and revenue alongside activation. This sacrifices immediacy and simplicity, and may reduce effort on signing new customers, but aligns the measure with the goal.

case.application: The structure of this case — a measure that predicted the goal until people were paid on it, a top performer whose results look too good, a leaderboard that turned colleagues into rivals, and a leader who must act before the facts are clear — transfers directly to player development and baseball operations. A development staff paid or promoted on how many players reach a level, or a scouting group judged on short-term statistical markers, faces the same decay of a once-informative measure. The same choices also recur: whether to suspend, investigate or redesign; how to protect people who did nothing wrong; and how to present uncertain numbers to ownership without overstating or hiding the problem.

questions.prompt: Across four regional offices of a hypothetical insurer, new hires in the claims role quit at twice the rate of new hires in other roles. Which inference is best supported before any further investigation?

options.text: The claims role attracts people with weaker commitment.
Something about the claims role — workload, measures, supervision or norms — is a likely contributor and should be examined first.
The recruiters hiring for claims are poor judges of character.
Turnover is random and nothing can be inferred.

questions.explanation: A pattern that recurs across many different people and offices in the same role is evidence about the role. Dispositional explanations are possible but should be tested after situational features shared by all those people are examined.

optionFeedback.a: This jumps to a dispositional explanation for a pattern that shared situational features explain more economically.
optionFeedback.c: Possible, but it is still a person-centred explanation that skips the shared role features.
optionFeedback.d: A consistent doubling across four offices is unlikely to be pure noise.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is most defensible?

stimulus.text: Fictional summary: An influential 2009 study (n = 40) reported that employees who first completed a tedious form persisted 40 percent less on a later puzzle. A 2024 preregistered replication across 18 laboratories (total n = 2,300) using the original materials found a difference of 2 percent, with a confidence interval spanning zero.

options.text: The original authors must have fabricated their data.
The original effect was probably inflated or absent; the preregistered multi-lab estimate is far more credible for practical decisions.
The two studies cancel out, so the true effect is about 21 percent.
The replication failed because laboratories differ; the original finding stands.

questions.explanation: A small study with a large reported effect is the profile of an inflated estimate; a large preregistered multi-lab test removes most analytic flexibility and estimates the effect precisely. Inflation does not require fraud, and averaging a tiny study with a huge one is not how evidence should be combined.

optionFeedback.a: Small samples, flexible analysis and publication filters can inflate effects without any misconduct.
optionFeedback.c: Studies should be weighted by precision; the multi-lab estimate dominates.
optionFeedback.d: Lab differences were part of the design and the pooled estimate is still near zero; the objection would need specific, testable conditions.

questions.prompt: Select every statement that is supported by this week’s evidence on motivation.

options.text: Expected, tangible rewards contingent on doing an interesting task tend to reduce later free-choice engagement in experiments.
Any payment for work destroys intrinsic motivation.
Intrinsic motivation remained a predictor of performance when incentives were present.
Positive verbal feedback tends to enhance intrinsic motivation.
Self-determination theory treats all extrinsic motivation as equally controlled.
Incentives were associated more with quantity of performance than with quality.

questions.explanation: The undermining effect is conditional on reward type and contingency; verbal feedback tends to help. The forty-year meta-analysis found intrinsic motivation remained predictive alongside incentives, with incentives more related to quantity. Self-determination theory explicitly distinguishes forms of extrinsic motivation, some of which are autonomous.

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of the proposal, and the best alternative?

stimulus.text: Hypothetical: at a public library system, experienced librarians have for years voluntarily mentored new staff. The director proposes paying $50 per completed mentoring session to “show we value it.”

options.text: No risk; paying for valued behavior always increases it.

Payment may reframe mentoring from professional contribution to a low-paid task and crowd out voluntary effort; recognition, protected time and a mentoring role in promotion criteria are lower-risk ways to show value.
The payment is too large and should be reduced to $10.
Mentoring should be made mandatory instead.

questions.explanation: Small payments for behavior sustained by professional norms risk replacing the norm with a price, as in the day-care example, and can signal that the task is unpleasant. Recognition and resources that support competence and relatedness show value without pricing the behavior.

optionFeedback.a: The crowding-out evidence shows payment does not always increase the paid behavior.
optionFeedback.c: A smaller payment does not avoid reframing and may make the task look less valued.
optionFeedback.d: Mandating it converts autonomous motivation into controlled motivation, the opposite of the goal.

questions.prompt: A salesperson has closed 92 units with ten days left in the quarter. The plan pays a $50 commission per unit plus a one-time $8,000 bonus if the quarter reaches 100 units. If she can pull exactly 8 units forward from next quarter, what is her average payoff per pulled-forward unit from the threshold bonus alone, in dollars? (Ignore the commission, which she earns in either quarter.)
questions.working: The bonus is earned only if she reaches 100. Pulling 8 units forward moves her from 92 to 100 and earns the $8,000 bonus. $8,000 ÷ 8 units = $1,000 per unit — twenty times the $50 commission. This is why thresholds create intense timing incentives near the cliff.
questions.explanation: Near the threshold, each unit moved across the quarter boundary is worth $8,000 divided by the 8 units needed, or $1,000, compared with $50 in commission. Threshold payout shapes concentrate incentive intensity near the target and invite timing games.

questions.prompt: You lead a team of software engineers. A new bonus on story points delivered per sprint has raised throughput by a third, but defect reports from customers are up and senior engineers have stopped reviewing others’ code. With a limited budget and a board that likes the throughput number, what is the best next move?

options.text: Raise the story-point bonus so that engineers can afford to spend time on reviews.
Keep the bonus but add a defect-rate penalty applied to each individual engineer.
Reduce the power of the story-point bonus, move part of it to a team-level measure that includes escaped defects, and protect code review in role expectations.
Abolish all incentives and return to the previous system without explanation.

questions.explanation: The multitask model predicts effort diversion from unmeasured tasks (review, quality) toward the paid one. Weakening the incentive on the narrow measure, broadening it at team level to include quality, and protecting review in the job design addresses the diversion without abandoning accountability.

optionFeedback.a: A stronger incentive on story points increases diversion away from unmeasured work.
optionFeedback.b: Individual defect penalties discourage taking on hard work and helping others, and invite hiding defects.
optionFeedback.d: Abolishing incentives silently forfeits the throughput gain and gives the board and team no rationale.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical regional bank pays branch staff a monthly bonus per new account opened, with self-reported data and a public leaderboard. Rank these redesigns from most to least likely to reduce unauthorized account openings while keeping a sales incentive.

options.text: Pay on accounts still active and funded after 90 days, verified by random audits, with the leaderboard removed.
Keep the per-account bonus but add a code-of-conduct training module.
Keep everything but double the number of accounts required for the bonus.
Pay on new accounts opened, but require a customer signature captured electronically.

questions.explanation: Paying on verified, durable outcomes with audits and no rivalry addresses the measure, the horizon and monitoring together. Requiring a verified customer signature closes the cheapest fabrication route but keeps a volume measure. Training changes nothing structural. Raising the target intensifies pressure on the same gameable measure and likely makes things worse.

questions.prompt: Identify the main flaw in this reasoning.

stimulus.text: Consultant’s slide: “Teams in the top quartile of psychological safety had 30 percent higher performance ratings from their own members. Therefore our psychological-safety workshop will raise your performance by 30 percent.”

options.text: It treats a cross-sectional, self-rated association as the causal effect of an intervention, and assumes the workshop changes safety by a full quartile.
Psychological safety has never been studied.
The comparison should have used the bottom quartile only.
Thirty percent is too small to matter.

questions.explanation: Same-source ratings inflate associations, performance may cause felt safety, and nothing shows the workshop changes safety, let alone by the amount separating quartiles. The meta-analytic evidence supports an association, not a causal effect of this size.

optionFeedback.b: Psychological safety has a sizeable literature, including a meta-analysis.
optionFeedback.c: Changing the comparison group does not fix the causal leap.
optionFeedback.d: The size is not the problem; the inference is.

questions.prompt: Two hospital departments receive the same 3 percent raise. Department A had been told raises would be frozen; Department B learned afterwards that a newly hired group received 8 percent. According to this week’s material, why might B react much worse?

options.text: B’s staff are more materialistic.
Fairness is judged against reference points and inferred intentions; B’s reference point is the new hires’ raise and the undisclosed difference may be read as disrespect.
The raise in B is objectively smaller.
People only care about absolute pay, so the reactions should be identical.

questions.explanation: The same amount is compared with different reference points — a freeze in A, a peer’s larger raise in B — and the way B learned of the difference invites an inference about intentions. Reciprocity responds to perceived kindness or unkindness, not only to amounts.

optionFeedback.a: A dispositional explanation ignores the different situations the two departments are in.
optionFeedback.c: The raises are identical in size.
optionFeedback.d: This contradicts the evidence that fairness judgments are relative and intention-sensitive.

questions.prompt: A team’s willingness to do unglamorous shared work has declined. Select every change that this week’s evidence suggests could help.

options.text: Address visible free riding promptly and consistently.
Introduce a public individual leaderboard on the shared work.
Have senior, high-status members visibly do the shared work.
Recognize contributions to shared work in ways peers can see and endorse.
Announce that anyone not contributing will be monitored by continuous tracking.
Ignore it; norms always recover on their own.

questions.explanation: Conditional cooperators withdraw when free riding goes unaddressed, so addressing it matters. Norms spread through visible behavior by high-status members, and informational, peer-endorsed recognition supports competence and relatedness. Leaderboards add rivalry; blanket surveillance signals distrust; norms that have begun to unravel do not reliably recover unaided.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical public school district plans to pay teachers a bonus based on the share of students passing a standardized test each spring. In 150–250 words, predict two intended and two unintended consequences, using at least two concepts from different lessons this week, and propose one design change that reduces an unintended consequence while keeping some accountability.
questions.modelAnswer: Intended: teachers will spend more effort on tested skills and on students near the passing line, and weak instruction in tested subjects may become visible. Unintended (multitask): effort will move away from untested subjects, deeper projects and students far above or below the passing threshold, because the measure pays only for crossing a line — a threshold payout shape. Unintended (gaming): some schools may narrow who sits the test or teach test formats rather than skills, so the pass rate decays as a measure of learning. A further risk (crowding out and reciprocity) is that teachers who see themselves as professionals may read individual pay on a single test as distrust, weakening voluntary effort such as mentoring colleagues. Design change: base a smaller, school-level bonus on growth across the full score distribution over two years, audited for test participation, combined with peer-reviewed professional goals. This keeps accountability while reducing the threshold incentive and the rivalry and distrust signals of individual pay.

rubric.criterion: Predicts intended and unintended consequences with mechanisms
levels: 2 — two intended and two unintended consequences, each tied to a mechanism

rubric.criterion: Uses concepts from at least two lessons correctly
levels: 2 — concepts from two or more lessons used correctly

rubric.criterion: Proposes a design change that targets a named side effect and keeps accountability
levels: 1 — change proposed but not linked to a side effect
2 — targeted change with its own likely trade-off noted

reserve.prompt: You chair a panel deciding which of five vendors to select. Given the conformity evidence, which procedure best protects independent judgment?

options.text: The most senior member states a view first to give the group direction.
Members submit written rankings independently before discussion; the chair speaks last.
Discuss openly and vote by show of hands.
Let the vendor with the most enthusiastic supporter win.

reserve.explanation: Conformity pressure is strongest when people hear a majority or high-status view before forming their own. Independent written judgments before discussion, with the chair last, preserve the information each member holds.

optionFeedback.a: A senior first view invites conformity toward it.
optionFeedback.c: Public voting after discussion adds visible conformity pressure.
optionFeedback.d: Enthusiasm is a social signal, not evidence.

reserve.prompt: Which incentive design fits this task best, given the evidence on incentives and intrinsic motivation?

stimulus.text: Hypothetical: a logistics firm needs warehouse staff to scan and shelve a backlog of 40,000 returned items in two weeks. The task is repetitive and staff report little interest in it. Accuracy can be checked automatically by scanner.

options.text: No incentive; intrinsic motivation will carry the work.
A direct per-item incentive with automatic accuracy checks, time-limited to the backlog.
A peer-recognition program only.
A ranking tournament where the bottom quartile loses shifts.

reserve.explanation: For low-interest, volume tasks with cheap quality checks, direct incentives raise quantity with little intrinsic motivation at stake. Automatic accuracy checks limit gaming, and time-limiting avoids converting an ongoing role into piece work.

optionFeedback.a: There is little intrinsic interest to rely on for this task.
optionFeedback.c: Recognition is valuable but weak for a short, repetitive volume push.
optionFeedback.d: Penalizing the bottom quartile adds rivalry and fear without a quality benefit.

reserve.prompt: Why do principals use incentive pay at all, according to agency theory?

options.text: Because agents are dishonest.
Because the principal cannot directly observe the agent’s effort and pays on outcomes correlated with it.
Because incentive pay is always cheaper than salary.
Because incentives eliminate the need for monitoring.

reserve.explanation: Incentive pay is a response to hidden action: when effort is unobservable, paying on correlated outcomes motivates effort. The cost is that pay then depends on noise and on what the measure misses.

optionFeedback.a: The model needs only divergent interests and hidden effort, not dishonesty.
optionFeedback.c: Incentive pay shifts risk to agents, who typically require compensation for bearing it.
optionFeedback.d: Incentives on imperfect measures increase the need to monitor for gaming.

reserve.prompt: Near-miss reports in your clinical laboratory have dropped to almost zero since a technician was disciplined after reporting a sample mix-up. What is the best next move?

options.text: Pay a bonus for each near-miss report.
Separate reporting from performance evaluation, make the response to honest error visibly non-punitive, and have senior staff report their own near-misses first.
Require every technician to file at least two reports per month.
Wait; reporting will recover once people forget the incident.

reserve.explanation: The drop is a predictable response to a punished messenger. Changing the consequences of reporting and having high-status members model the norm addresses the cause. Paying per report or setting quotas invites trivial or fabricated reports.

optionFeedback.a: Paying per report risks pricing a professional norm and inviting low-value reports.
optionFeedback.c: Quotas turn reporting into a gameable count.
optionFeedback.d: Norms reinforced by a visible punishment rarely recover on their own.

assignment.title: Incentive Misalignment Audit: The Mesa Verde Condors

brief.text: The Mesa Verde Condors are a fictional professional baseball organization with a major-league club, several minor-league affiliates, an amateur scouting department, an international program, a player-development staff and a research and analytics group. Use only generic, hypothetical situations; do not draw on confidential information or the practices of any real organization. Invent the specific measures and pay arrangements you analyze, stating them as assumptions.

Your task is to audit the organization’s incentive structure and identify at least three plausible misalignments between groups — for example between amateur scouting and player development, between player development and the major-league coaching staff, or between front-office metrics and what any of these groups are asked to do. For each, explain the mechanism using this week’s concepts, propose a redesign, and predict the side effects of your redesign honestly. A redesign that creates no new problem has not been examined carefully enough.

items: Possible measures to consider (invent and state your own): signing-class outcomes credited to scouts; the number of players promoted or reaching the majors credited to development staff; short-term statistical improvement credited to coaches; win–loss and individual statistics at affiliates; report volume or model adoption credited to analysts; budget adherence credited to department heads.
Possible levers: what is measured, whose performance counts, horizon and deferral, payout shape, monitoring and discretion, status and recognition, decision rights.
Remember the social economy: reciprocity between departments, norms about sharing information, fairness of credit, and whether staff can safely report that something is not working.

brief.text: Write as an internal memo to a fictional general manager. Data, if any, must be labelled synthetic.

assignment.deliverable: A 900–1,400-word memo identifying three incentive misalignments in a fictional baseball organization, with mechanisms, redesigns and predicted side effects.

template.heading: Summary and recommendation
template.guidance: In three to five sentences, state the three misalignments and the single redesign you would prioritize first, and why.

template.heading: Assumed incentive structure
template.guidance: Describe the measures, rewards, horizons and decision rights you are assuming for each group. Make clear these are hypothetical.

template.heading: Misalignment 1–3: mechanism
template.guidance: For each misalignment, describe what is rewarded, what is hoped for, and the mechanism (multitask diversion, gaming, crowding out, free riding, fairness, status). Cite course concepts.

template.heading: Redesigns
template.guidance: For each misalignment, propose a specific change in measure, unit, horizon, payout shape, monitoring or non-financial levers. Explain why it should help.

template.heading: Predicted side effects and how you would detect them
template.guidance: For each redesign, name the most likely new problem (new gaming route, cost, weaker effort, fairness concerns) and the early-warning signal you would watch.

template.heading: Evidence and uncertainty
template.guidance: Distinguish which parts of your reasoning rest on robust evidence, which on theory, and which on your own judgment. Say what information would change your recommendation.

prompts: Recall a time you attributed a colleague’s behavior to their character. What situational feature — measure, norm, status, friction — might have produced the same behavior in most people? What would you do differently now?
Which parts of your own work do you do for intrinsic reasons, and which for external ones? Has any reward, metric or evaluation ever changed how you felt about work you used to enjoy?
Identify one measure in your professional world that you think has started to decay under pressure. Who benefits from it continuing to be used, and what would it cost to replace it?
When did you last see someone in a meeting hold back a dissenting view? What about the situation made dissent costly, and what could the person chairing have changed?

review.front: What does it suggest when the same performance problem recurs across different people in the same role?
review.back: That features of the role or situation — measures, norms, status, friction — are likely contributors and should be examined before individual character.

review.front: Summarize the meta-analytic evidence on conformity in Asch-type tasks.
review.back: Robust but variable: larger with larger majorities and in more collectivist cultures, and declining in U.S. samples over the decades after Asch.

review.front: What did the 2015 Open Science Collaboration find about replication effect sizes?
review.back: Replication effects averaged roughly half the original estimates; far fewer replications than originals were significant, and social psychology replicated less often than cognitive psychology.

review.front: What happened when ego depletion was tested in a preregistered multi-lab replication?
review.back: The pooled effect was close to zero; the popular “willpower runs out” claim lacks reliable support.

review.front: Name the three basic needs proposed by self-determination theory.
review.back: Autonomy, competence and relatedness.

review.front: Which rewards most reliably undermined free-choice intrinsic motivation in experiments?
review.back: Expected, tangible rewards contingent on doing, completing or performing the task. Verbal positive feedback tended to enhance it; unexpected rewards had little effect.

review.front: What happened after a fine for late pickup was introduced at Israeli day-care centers?
review.back: Late pickups rose and stayed high after the fine was removed — the price replaced a moral obligation.

review.front: According to the forty-year meta-analysis, how do intrinsic motivation and incentives relate to performance?
review.back: They jointly predict it; intrinsic motivation remained predictive with incentives present, relates more to quality, and matters less when incentives are directly tied to performance. Incentives relate more to quantity.

review.front: Why do principals use incentive pay, and what does it cost?
review.back: Effort is unobservable, so they pay on correlated outcomes. The cost: pay depends on luck and on whatever the measure misses.

review.front: State the multitask problem in one sentence.
review.back: Strong incentives on easily measured tasks pull effort from hard-to-measure ones, so weaker incentives or job redesign can be optimal.

review.front: Why does a measure decay once pay depends on it?
review.back: People find cheaper ways to move the measure than to move the goal, so the measure’s correlation with the goal weakens (Goodhart’s and Campbell’s laws).

review.front: What behavior does a threshold (cliff) bonus invite?
review.back: Shifting results across periods near the threshold and easing off when the target is far above or out of reach.

review.front: What happens to cooperation in repeated public-goods games with and without sanctions?
review.back: Without sanctions it typically declines as conditional cooperators withdraw; with the option to punish free riders it can be sustained.

review.front: Why can identical raises feel fair in one unit and unfair in another?
review.back: Fairness is judged against reference points (prior pay, peers, expectations) and inferred intentions, not only amounts.

review.front: What is the main limitation of the evidence that psychological safety improves performance?
review.back: Most studies are cross-sectional and same-source, so causal direction and common-method bias are unresolved.

weeks.title: How to Know What Is True
weeks.question: When a study, a dashboard or a trusted colleague says something works, how do you decide how much to believe it and what to do about it?

overview.text: Executives are paid to act on evidence they did not produce: analyses from their staff, studies from consultants and vendors, research from universities, and the apparent lessons of their own experience. Most of that evidence is neither worthless nor conclusive. This week builds the skills to tell the difference and to act sensibly in between.

The week moves in five steps. Lesson 1 separates signal from noise: regression to the mean, confidence intervals, p-values and power, and the Bayesian logic that connects them to Week 1’s base rates. Lesson 2 examines the replication crisis as a system — flexible analysis, low power and selective publication — that operates inside organizations as well as in journals. Lesson 3 is a compact course in causal inference for executives: counterfactuals, confounding and selection, randomized trials, and the quasi-experimental designs that have transformed economics and policy evaluation. Lesson 4 adds the questions that remain after a design is credible: effect size, measurement, Goodhart’s law, external validity and survivorship. Lesson 5 asks how to combine imperfect evidence, using evidence hierarchies and meta-analysis without being ruled by them.

The Evidence Lab lets you generate thousands of simulated studies and watch exaggerated effects, false positives and missed effects emerge from design choices. The case, set in a health system, puts two respected executives on opposite sides of the same data. The assignment asks you to critique a real published study with a structured rubric. The aim is not cynicism. It is calibrated belief: knowing how much a piece of evidence should move you, and how to design your organization’s decisions so that it learns.

objectives: Distinguish signal from noise using regression to the mean, confidence intervals, p-values and statistical power.
Explain how researcher degrees of freedom, low power and publication bias produce exaggerated and false findings, and evaluate remedies.
Identify confounding, selection and collider bias and match randomized and quasi-experimental designs to causal questions.
Critique a study’s effect size, measurement, external validity and susceptibility to metric gaming.
Combine several imperfect lines of evidence into a stated degree of belief and a proportionate decision.

concepts.name: p-values: what they are and are not
Type M and type S errors

lessons.title: Signal, Noise and the Meaning of p
lessons.summary: Every measurement mixes signal with noise; regression to the mean, confidence intervals, p-values and power are tools for keeping the two apart.
objectives: Explain regression to the mean and identify it in a performance story that offers a causal explanation instead.
Interpret a confidence interval and a p-value correctly and state what each does not tell you.
Use statistical power and prior plausibility to judge how much a significant result should change your belief.
lessons.executive: Most numbers that reach your desk are a true level plus luck. When you select people, units or quarters because they were extreme, the luck you selected on will not repeat, so they drift back toward average whatever you do: regression to the mean. A p-value tells you how surprising the data would be if nothing were going on; it does not tell you the probability the claim is true, how big the effect is, or whether it matters. Ask for the estimate with its confidence interval, the sample size, and how plausible the claim was before the data. Treat a small study’s significant result as a hypothesis, not a finding.

explore.text: A regional hospital system ranks its twenty emergency departments every quarter on door-to-provider time. The three worst departments are placed on an improvement plan: a consultant visits, managers attend a workshop, and dashboards are posted in the break rooms. Next quarter, all three improve markedly. The three best departments, which received a congratulatory letter, all get worse. The chief operating officer concludes that improvement plans work and that praise breeds complacency. This scenario is hypothetical, but the pattern is everywhere.

Before reading on: what would you expect to happen to the three worst departments next quarter if the improvement plan had done nothing at all? Write down a number of departments (0–3) you would expect to improve, and why.

Tversky and Kahneman described the same pattern in flight training. Instructors noticed that cadets who were praised after an unusually smooth landing usually did worse on the next attempt, while cadets criticized after a rough landing usually improved. The instructors concluded that criticism works and praise backfires. The authors’ point was that the instructors had discovered regression to the mean and mistaken it for a causal effect of their feedback ([Tversky & Kahneman, 1974](R-tversky-1974-judgment)).

This lesson is about the difference between signal and noise. It covers four tools that every executive who reads evidence must handle comfortably: regression to the mean, the confidence interval, the p-value and statistical power. None of them requires advanced mathematics. All of them are misunderstood by many of the people who will present evidence to you.

understand.text: Observed performance is a true level plus luck

Think of any measured result — a department’s quarterly wait time, a fund’s annual return, a salesperson’s monthly bookings, a hitter’s batting average over three weeks — as the sum of two parts: a stable underlying level and a transient component that does not repeat. The transient part includes genuine randomness, measurement error, and temporary circumstances such as a flu outbreak or an easy schedule. The proportion of variation that is stable is called the *reliability* of the measure. When reliability is high, last period predicts next period well. When it is low, last period is mostly noise.

Now select units because they were extreme. The worst three departments are, on average, departments with a somewhat worse true level *and* a bad draw of luck in that quarter. Next quarter the true level persists but the luck is redrawn, so on average they move back toward the middle. The same is true in reverse for the best performers. Regression to the mean is not a force and it does not require any intervention. It is a consequence of selecting on a noisy measure. The lower the reliability and the more extreme the selection, the larger the expected regression.

understand.caption: Why selected extremes drift back

steps.label: Measure
steps.text: Observed result = true level + transient noise

steps.label: Select
steps.text: Pick the extreme cases on the observed result

steps.label: Hidden bias
steps.text: Selected cases carry unusually large noise in the selected direction

steps.label: Re-measure
steps.text: Noise is redrawn; the true level remains

steps.label: Drift
steps.text: The group moves toward the average with or without any intervention

understand.text: A simple prediction rule follows. Your best forecast of next period is not last period’s observed value but a weighted average of it and the group mean, with the weight on the observed value equal to the measure’s reliability. If a quarterly metric has a reliability of 0.4, a department that was 10 minutes worse than average should be expected to be about 4 minutes worse next quarter. If the improvement plan produces a 6-minute gain, most of it was expected anyway. The only clean way to know whether the plan did anything is to compare treated departments with similarly extreme departments that were not treated, ideally chosen at random.

understand.title: Prerequisite: samples, sampling variability and the standard error

blocks.text: A *sample* is the subset of cases you actually observe; the *population* is the larger set you want to learn about. If you surveyed a different random sample, you would get a different average. That variation from sample to sample is *sampling variability*. Its typical size is the *standard error*: roughly the standard deviation of individual cases divided by the square root of the sample size. Quadrupling a sample halves the standard error. This square-root law is why small samples bounce around so much and why doubling a pilot’s size buys less precision than intuition suggests.

Two numbers therefore always travel together: the estimate (for example, a 3-point improvement) and its uncertainty (for example, a standard error of 2 points). An estimate without its uncertainty is half a fact.

understand.text: Confidence intervals

A 95% confidence interval is a range constructed by a procedure that, across many repeated samples, would capture the true value 95% of the time. In practice, read it as the range of effect sizes reasonably compatible with the data under the analysis assumptions. Two features matter more than whether it excludes zero. Its *location* tells you the most plausible magnitudes. Its *width* tells you how much the study actually taught you. An interval from −1 to +9 minutes and an interval from +3.8 to +4.2 minutes can both have the same center; only the second one supports a confident operational decision.
What a p-value is, and is not

A p-value is the probability of obtaining data at least as extreme as what was observed, *if* a specified statistical model — usually one in which the true effect is zero — were correct, and if all its assumptions held. In 2016 the American Statistical Association issued its first formal statement on a matter of statistical practice to correct widespread misuse. Among its principles: p-values can indicate how incompatible data are with a specified model; they do not measure the probability that the hypothesis is true or that the data arose by chance alone; decisions should not rest only on whether a p-value crosses a threshold; proper inference requires full reporting; and a p-value does not measure the size or importance of an effect ([Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016](R-wasserstein-2016-asa)).

understand.caption: Statements about “p = .03”: which are correct?
rows: If there were truly no effect and the model were right, data this extreme would arise about 3% of the time.
There is a 3% chance the result is a fluke.
That is a statement about the hypothesis given the data; the p-value is about the data given the hypothesis.
There is a 97% chance the effect is real.
That probability depends on prior plausibility and power, which the p-value ignores.
The effect is large or important.
A tiny effect in a huge sample can produce a tiny p-value.
A replication would be significant 97% of the time.
The probability of replication depends on the true effect and the replication’s power.
p = .06 means there is no effect.
Absence of significance is not evidence of absence, especially in small samples.
understand.note: Original teaching table based on the principles in the ASA statement.

understand.text: Power: the probability of detecting what is really there

*Statistical power* is the probability that a study will produce a significant result when a true effect of a given size exists. It depends on the size of the effect, the noise in the measure, the sample size and the significance threshold. A study of 20 people per group looking for a modest effect (about a third of a standard deviation) has power of roughly 15%: it will miss the true effect about 85% of the time. Low power has a less obvious cost, taken up in [Lesson 2](#w04-l2): when a low-powered study does reach significance, its estimate is usually far too large.

understand.caption: Approximate power to detect a true effect of d = 0.3 (two-sided, p < .05)
understand.note: Synthetic illustration computed from the standard two-sample formula and simulation; values rounded.

understand.title: Methodological note: why the p-value is not the probability you want

blocks.text: The question an executive cares about is: given this result, how likely is it that the effect is real? That is a *posterior* probability. Bayes’ rule says it depends on three things: the prior probability that the tested idea is true, the power of the study, and the significance threshold. Suppose your analytics team tests 100 product ideas, of which perhaps 10 genuinely work. With power of 50% and a 5% threshold, about 5 of the 10 real effects come back significant, and about 4.5 of the 90 null ideas come back significant by chance. Roughly half of the “wins” are false. Raise power to 80% and only 8 of about 12.5 wins are real; lower the prior to 1 in 100 and false wins dominate.

This is the logic of Ioannidis’s argument that, under realistic priors, power and bias, many claimed findings in some fields are likely to be false ([Ioannidis, 2005](R-ioannidis-2005-most)). It also explains why the same p-value should move you more for a plausible, mechanistically grounded claim than for a surprising one. Week 1’s base-rate reasoning is the same arithmetic applied to research.

challenge.text: Three objections deserve a serious answer. First, some argue that p-values are fine and the problem is misinterpretation, so better training rather than new methods is the remedy. That is partly right: a p-value correctly understood is a legitimate measure of surprise under a model. But a tool that is routinely misread by trained researchers is a poor tool for executive communication. Estimates with intervals carry the same information and more.

Second, Bayesian analysts argue that executives should ask for posterior probabilities directly. That is attractive, but priors can be chosen to flatter a conclusion, and a Bayesian analysis with a hidden prior is no more transparent than a frequentist one with a hidden analysis plan. The disciplined position is to ask for the prior to be stated and for the result to be shown under a skeptical prior as well.

Third, not everything that drifts toward the mean is regression. Interventions can work, and true levels can change. The ASA statement’s emphasis on context and on full reporting is a reminder that statistical tools never substitute for design: the question is always what the comparison group was ([Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016](R-wasserstein-2016-asa)).

challenge.title: Executive twist: the board wants a yes or no

blocks.text: You chair a review of a pilot in a financial-services contact center. The pilot reduced complaint rates by an estimated 11%, with a 95% interval from −2% to +23%. The p-value is 0.09. The vendor calls it “directionally positive”; your finance lead calls it “not significant, so it failed”. Both are reasoning from the threshold. The interval says the program could plausibly do nothing or could do a great deal. The decision turns on costs: if extending the pilot is cheap and reversible, buying more information is worth it; if full rollout is expensive and hard to undo, it is not yet justified. Your job is to reframe the decision around the range of plausible effects and the cost of being wrong in each direction, not around p.

apply.text: Player development is an ideal environment for regression to the mean, because nearly every early-season statistic has low reliability and nearly every intervention is triggered by an extreme. A hitter who opens the season badly is given a mechanical adjustment and a new routine; three weeks later he has improved and the adjustment gets the credit. A pitcher with an exceptional first month is promoted and then “struggles to adjust to the level”. Some of each story may be true. The disciplined question is how much improvement or decline you would have predicted with no intervention, given the reliability of the measure over that sample.

items: Before an intervention, record the forecast for the player without it (the observed value shrunk toward his own longer-run baseline or the group mean).
Judge the intervention by performance relative to that forecast, not relative to the slump.
Where possible, compare with similarly extreme players who did not receive the intervention, or randomize which players receive it first.
Prefer process measures with higher reliability over short-sample outcomes when you need to judge quickly.

apply.text: The same discipline applies in other domains. A government agency that audits the schools with the worst test scores will see improvement next year; a private-equity firm that replaces the managers of its worst-performing portfolio companies will see recoveries; an asset manager that hires last year’s top fund will often be disappointed. In each case the honest benchmark is the regression-adjusted forecast, not last year’s extreme.

Worked problem: a quarterly employee-engagement score has a reliability of 0.5 across teams. A team scores 20 points below the company average and receives coaching. Next quarter it is 6 points below average. How much of the 14-point improvement would you have expected without coaching? (Answer: about 10 points, because the expected position is 0.5 × −20 = −10. The coaching is credited with at most about 4 points, and even that needs a comparison group.)

retain.text: Observed results combine a stable level with transient noise. Selecting on extremes guarantees drift back toward the mean, which looks like an effect of whatever you did in between. A p-value measures surprise under a null model, not the truth of a claim or the size of an effect; confidence intervals and power tell you how much a study can teach you. How much a significant result should move you depends on prior plausibility and power.
Explain to a colleague, in two sentences, why the worst performers on a noisy metric usually improve.
List three things a p-value does not tell you.
Why does the same p-value deserve less belief when power is low and the hypothesis is surprising?

takeaways: Selecting on extremes of a noisy measure produces regression to the mean with or without any intervention.
Judge an intervention against a regression-adjusted forecast or a comparison group, never against the slump that triggered it.
A p-value is the probability of data this extreme under a null model — not the probability the claim is true, and not a measure of importance.
Ask for estimates with confidence intervals, sample sizes and power; the interval’s width shows how much was learned.
The credibility of a significant result depends on prior plausibility and power, as Bayes’ rule makes explicit.

check.prompt: A sales organization gives its bottom-decile reps an intensive coaching program. Their bookings rise substantially the next quarter. What is the most important missing piece of information?

options.text: The satisfaction scores the reps gave the coaching program.
How much similarly ranked reps who were not coached improved over the same period.
Whether the improvement was statistically significant.
Whether top-decile reps declined over the same period.

check.explanation: Bottom-decile reps were selected partly for bad luck, so they would be expected to improve without coaching. Only a comparison with similarly extreme reps who were not coached separates the coaching effect from regression to the mean. Significance of the before-after change would not help, because the regression itself is a real, systematic change.

optionFeedback.a: Satisfaction with a program is not evidence of its effect on bookings.
optionFeedback.c: A before-after change can be highly significant and still be entirely regression to the mean.
optionFeedback.d: Decline at the top is what regression predicts too; it does not isolate the coaching effect.

check.prompt: A study reports a difference with p = .02. Select every statement that is correct.

options.text: If there were no true difference and the model were correct, results at least this extreme would occur about 2% of the time.
There is a 98% probability that the difference is real.
The result says nothing by itself about whether the difference is large enough to matter.
If the study had low power, the estimated difference is more likely than usual to be exaggerated.
A replication with the same design would be significant about 98% of the time.

check.explanation: Option a is the definition of a p-value. Option c follows from the ASA principle that p-values do not measure effect size or importance. Option d anticipates type-M error: in low-powered studies only overestimates clear the threshold. Options b and e confuse the p-value with the probability of the hypothesis or of replication.
