components.title: Decision rights

guidance.text: Most coordination failures in Exhibit 6 are decision-rights failures: nobody owned roster-change updates, nobody decided what goes on page one, nobody approved data sharing. Assign roles for the decisions that create or destroy the most value, not for every task.

Use a vocabulary such as Recommend, Input, Decide and Informed (the Builder’s labels, adapted from the consulting RAPID framework). It is a practitioner heuristic with anecdotal support, useful because it forces one name into the “Decide” box; it is not evidence that clarity alone improves results.
Watch the boundary between Input and veto. If the hitting coach’s Input can stop a report, he holds a hidden Decide. Name those cases or remove them.
Which decision would you most like to Decide but should only Recommend? Write down why the person who Decides will accept your recommendation more often if you do not claim the call.

components.title: Budget and resource allocation

guidance.text: Your budget has three parts that behave differently: a recurring personnel envelope, a small operating line, and a one-time investment fund for three-year projects. Do not mix them. Recurring commitments are hard to reverse; one-time investments can be staged.

Use the Capital Allocation Lab to compare the eight candidate investments by net present value, internal rate of return, payback and profitability index, and to see the best portfolio within the $1,000,000 fund. Then interrogate it. Most of the benefit streams depend on finance’s run-value convention; switch scenarios and watch which projects survive. A project whose value is entirely hours saved is more robust than one whose value is entirely runs.

Expect your estimates to be optimistic. Kahneman and Lovallo describe how planners take the inside view of one project and neglect the distribution of outcomes for similar ones. Before accepting any benefit figure, ask what share of comparable technology rollouts or new departments hit their first-year targets, and adjust.

guidance.text: Some projects should be funded even with a negative NPV, for example data governance if counsel concludes it is required. Say so explicitly rather than inflating its benefits to make the numbers work.

components.title: Technology and analytical infrastructure

guidance.text: Exhibit 5 is a build-versus-buy decision with a political edge. Evaluate it on four axes: time to value (spring training or July), control and ownership of code and models, dependence (on a vendor or on another department), and the contractual terms that govern data use and exit.

Adoption will decide whether any option works. Lab experiments found that people who watched an algorithm err became less willing to rely on it than on a human forecaster, even when the algorithm was better; a later series found that letting users adjust the output, even within narrow limits, sharply increased use. Other experiments found the opposite default among lay people, algorithm appreciation, while experienced professionals discounted algorithmic advice. The honest reading: reactions depend on who the users are and whether they have seen errors, and veteran coaches who will see the first public miss are the worrying case.

guidance.caption: Designing for the first visible error

steps.label: Before launch
steps.text: Tell coaches the expected error rate and what a miss will look like.

steps.label: Bounded override
steps.text: Let coaches adjust within stated limits and record the adjustment.

steps.label: First miss
steps.text: Review it openly within 48 hours; separate bad luck from bad model.

steps.label: Learn
steps.text: Compare model, override and outcome over many cases, not one.

guidance.text: Treat data governance as infrastructure, not paperwork: access tiers, device management, logging and retention are design decisions you make now. Check vendor terms with counsel before you commit; the July incident in Exhibit 6 is a license problem as well as a security one.

prompts: Which technology option do you choose, and what must be true by Opening Day for it to succeed?
How will coaches be able to adjust or override outputs, and how will you learn from overrides?
What happens to your infrastructure if the vendor raises prices or Research and Analytics reprioritizes?

components.title: Stakeholder engagement

guidance.text: Map each stakeholder by power over your success, interest in your work and current stance. A power and interest grid is a practitioner heuristic, not a measured model; its value is forcing you to write down assumptions you can test in conversation.

Network position matters, and the right position depends on the change. In a field study of change initiatives in a national health system, change agents with ties to potential resisters did better on some kinds of change and not others; how far the change departed from established norms moderated which networks helped. A department that reorganizes how coaches prepare is a divergent change for many of them.

guidance.caption: Interest behind the position (fill in)
rows: A named role in the meeting
His knowledge and the coaches’ trust

guidance.text: Use Week 7’s distinction between positions and interests: most of these leaders are negotiating, even if nobody calls it that. Plan the order of conversations, what you will trade, and what you will not trade.
Who is the highest-power neutral in your map? What is the first conversation you will have with that person, and what will you ask rather than tell?

prompts: Who are the three stakeholders whose opposition would sink the department, and what does each need?
What will you trade with Research and Analytics, and what is your walk-away?
How will you protect Ernesto Villalba’s standing while changing the meeting he runs?

components.title: Legal and ethical considerations

guidance.text: Educational material about general legal concepts — not legal advice. Consult a qualified attorney about any specific agreement or data practice. In this capstone, your job is to spot issues and frame questions for counsel, not to resolve them.

Separate three kinds of data. Opponent data is mostly public or licensed; the issues are contractual (license scope, sharing, storage, exit). Your own players’ performance data is sensitive and governed by agreements and club policy. Health and biometric data is the most sensitive: comprehensive privacy regimes such as the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation treat data concerning health as a special category and require purpose limitation and data minimisation. The GDPR appears here only as an example of a strict regime; whether any regime applies to a given player is a question for counsel.

A neutral way to structure your governance plan is the NIST Privacy Framework’s functions: identify what data you hold and why, govern it with policy and roles, control processing, communicate with the people the data describes, and protect it. It is voluntary guidance, not a statement of what any law requires.

guidance.caption: Issue-spotting starter (questions for counsel, not conclusions)
rows: July report forwarded outside the club
What do current licenses permit for sharing, storage and devices?
Recovery marker in a coaches’ report
Who may see readiness data, for what purpose, under the agreement and policy?
Which law governs collection and transfer of their data?
Do role changes alter terms, reporting or confidentiality obligations?
Models built with Research and Analytics
Who owns code and models built jointly or by contractors?

guidance.text: Ethics goes beyond compliance. Ask who bears the risk of each use of data, whether the player would recognize the use as fair, and what you would do if a coach asked for something lawful but corrosive to trust. Write down the line you will hold before someone asks you to cross it.

prompts: Which data uses will you refuse in Year 1 even if they are lawful, and why?
What questions will you take to counsel before signing any vendor contract?
How will you handle data about academy players who are minors?
Who in your structure is accountable for a data incident?

components.title: Organizational communication

guidance.text: Exhibit 6’s June incident, a warning on page 17, is a communication design failure. The research on information overload across organizational fields describes a consistent pattern: beyond a point, more information lowers decision quality, and the remedy is filtering, structure and timing rather than effort.

Meetings have their own failure mode. In hidden-profile experiments, groups discussed information everyone already shared and neglected information held by one member. Your pre-series meeting is a hidden-profile setting: the road scout, the catcher and the analyst each know different things. Structure the meeting so unique information is asked for by name.
Translation is not an afterthought. A report a player cannot read comfortably is a report he did not receive. Budget the time and assign the owner.

prompts: What is on page one of the coaches’ brief, and who decides?
How will your pre-series meeting surface what only one person knows?
What is the bilingual standard, and who checks it?

components.title: Performance indicators

guidance.text: Choose a small set of indicators that tell you whether the department is working and that you would be comfortable having people optimize. Kerr’s classic essay shows that organizations get the behavior they reward, not the behavior they hope for; Campbell warned that the more an indicator is used for consequential decisions, the more it is corrupted and the more it distorts the activity it monitors.

guidance.caption: A balanced indicator set (example structure)
rows: Share of briefs delivered by deadline
Share of recommendations discussed in the pre-series meeting
Accuracy of positioning and pitch-mix forecasts, scored after the series
Proper scoring rule such as the Brier score
Coach and player survey, twice a season
Report with intervals, not point estimates
Runs or outs in situations the department targeted
Multi-season view; never a bonus trigger

guidance.text: Resist the temptation to promise wins or runs as a Year 1 indicator. With dozens of series and noisy outcomes, any estimate of the department’s effect on run prevention will be imprecise; report it, but do not let it decide the department’s fate in October.

prompts: Which three indicators would you show the president in October, and what would each look like if the department were failing?
How could your own staff game each indicator, and what counterweight prevents it?
Which indicator would you refuse to tie to compensation, and why?

components.title: Research and evidence standards

guidance.text: Your department’s product is evidence, so it needs written standards for what counts as evidence. Evidence-based management, as Rousseau framed it, combines the best available research with local data, professional judgment and the values of those affected. It is a discipline of transparency about each source, not deference to any single one.

Two standards matter most for a small department. First, separate prediction from postdiction: write down before the season what result would count as success for a new practice, and label everything else exploratory. Second, distrust large effects from small samples: when studies or seasons are small and noisy, the estimates that look impressive tend to exaggerate the true effect and can have the wrong sign.

guidance.caption: Evidence labels for every recommendation
rows: Replicated research or multi-season internal evidence
Platoon tendencies of a long-tenured hitter
A new reliever’s pitch mix over 60 pitches
Expert observation not yet in the data
Road scout sees a changed delivery
A sequencing idea for a hitter new to the league

guidance.text: Agree with Research and Analytics on who reviews whose work. A simple rule, that any claim that drives a structural change is reviewed by someone outside the team that produced it, protects both departments.

prompts: What evidence labels will appear on your reports, and who assigns them?
What will you write down before Opening Day about how you will evaluate the department’s own impact?
How will you handle a coach’s observation that contradicts the data?

components.title: Change management strategy

guidance.text: Kotter’s eight steps are the vocabulary most executives know: urgency, guiding coalition, vision, communication, empowerment, short-term wins, consolidation, culture. Treat them as a practitioner heuristic drawn from consulting observation, with limited direct testing and a linear sequence that rarely matches real change.

The broader quantitative literature on how employees react to change points to process variables you control: participation in shaping the change, quality and timing of information, and trust in the people leading it, along with how the change affects each person. Those levers fit a coaching staff better than slogans about urgency.

guidance.caption: Pace and participation
cells: Drift: little resistance, little change
Co-design: slower start, durable adoption
Imposition: quick launch, fragile
Sprint with a coalition: demanding, possible before spring training

guidance.text: Plan the first visible win and the first visible failure. The win should be something coaches feel within two weeks of spring training (for example, briefs that arrive on time and fit on two pages). The failure will come; decide now how you will review it openly without blame, because staff report errors only where it feels safe to do so.

prompts: Where on the pace and participation matrix will you operate, and why there?
What is your first visible win, and when will coaches notice it?
How will you respond to the first public error?
What will you not change in Year 1 to keep trust?

components.title: First 90-day implementation plan

guidance.text: Your 90 days run from your appointment in November to about February 10, the eve of spring training. They contain a hard deadline (January 20), a budget lock (January 31) and a hiring market that closes in mid-December. Sequence by dependency: you cannot finalize staffing before the structure, or the structure before the key decision-rights conversations.

steps.label: Days 1–20: listen
steps.text: Interviews with coaches, department heads, counsel; validate the exhibits.

steps.label: Days 15–35: decide structure
steps.text: Choose structure, offer first hires before mid-December.

steps.label: Days 30–60: agree rights
steps.text: Decision rights with the manager and Research and Analytics; data policy with counsel.

steps.label: Days 55–70: present
steps.text: January 20 strategy; January 31 budget lock.

steps.label: Days 70–90: rehearse
steps.text: Dry-run briefs on spring-training opponents; fix delivery.

guidance.text: First-90-day frameworks for new leaders are practitioner heuristics. The useful parts are generic: learn before you change, secure early agreement on expectations with your boss, and pick early wins that build credibility for harder changes later.
For each workstream, name an owner, a dependency, a deadline and the signal that it is off track. A plan with no signals will tell you it is fine until it is not.

prompts: What must be true by January 20, and what can wait until spring training?
Which dependency is most likely to slip, and what is your fallback?

components.title: Longer-term strategic roadmap

guidance.text: A new department runs on assumptions, not facts. Discovery-driven planning proposes organizing a roadmap around the assumptions that must be true, with milestones where those assumptions are tested before more resources are committed. It is a practitioner method with little controlled evidence, but it fits a department whose value case is unproven.

guidance.caption: A gated three-year roadmap (example structure)
rows: Coaches use the brief and rate it usable
Redesign the product before adding staff
Forecast accuracy beats last season’s baseline
International coverage changes preparation for new players

guidance.text: Make reversibility explicit. Some Year 1 choices, such as a three-year vendor contract or moving people out of other departments, are expensive to undo. A roadmap that stages irreversible choices behind evidence is easier to defend than one that commits everything in January.

prompts: What are the three assumptions your department most depends on, and when will you test each?
Which Year 1 commitments are hard to reverse, and why are they worth it?
What would cause you to recommend shrinking the department?

components.title: Risk register and alternative scenarios

guidance.text: Start with a premortem: imagine it is October and the department has failed, and have each person you trust write down why. The technique is a practitioner method with limited controlled evidence, but it legitimizes dissent and surfaces risks people otherwise keep to themselves.

guidance.caption: Risk register format
rows: Manager disengages after an early miss

guidance.text: Then write two or three alternative scenarios: coherent stories about how the year could unfold differently, for example a manager change in June, a 15% budget cut, or a breakthrough in coach adoption. For each, state what you would do differently and which early signal would tell you it is happening. Use the outside view when estimating likelihoods: how often do new analytical units or technology rollouts hit their first-year plans?

prompts: What are the five risks most likely to end the department in Year 1?
What early signal would tell you each is happening?
Describe one scenario in which your strategy is wrong, and what you would do.
Which risk will you accept without mitigation, and why?

components.title: Executive presentation

guidance.text: Your audience is two senior leaders with forty minutes and many other priorities. Lead with the recommendation and the decision you need from them, then the reasons, then the risks. Answer-first structures (for example, BLUF) are practitioner heuristics; they work because a busy reader gets the decision even if attention runs out early.

Information overload lowers decision quality. Cut every slide that does not change the decision, and move detail to an appendix or the memo. A useful test: could Castellanos explain your recommendation to ownership in two sentences after the meeting?

guidance.caption: A ten-slide spine (example)
rows: Diagnosis with evidence and its limits
Top risks and what we will not do

guidance.text: Rehearse the transitions and the time. At about 130 to 150 words per minute, a ten-minute talk is roughly 1,300 to 1,500 words; leave most of the meeting for questions.

prompts: What exact decisions are you asking the president and GM to make?

components.title: Written defense of major decisions

guidance.text: Pick the four to six decisions that a skeptic would attack hardest, and write the strongest case against each before you write your reply. Meta-analytic evidence from mostly laboratory studies found that structured dissent methods such as devil’s advocacy produced better decisions than accepting an expert recommendation uncritically.

Write the defense before you know what the president thinks. Research on accountability finds that expecting to justify a decision to an audience whose views are unknown, before deciding, promotes more careful and self-critical reasoning; accountability to a known audience tends to produce conformity, and accountability after the fact tends to produce defensive justification.

guidance.caption: Structure for each decision
rows: What you chose, in one sentence
Stated as its best advocate would state it
Evidence, reasoning and what you concede
A probability that the decision is right, recorded in the Decision Journal

guidance.text: Concede where you should. A defense that concedes a real weakness and shows how you will monitor it is more credible than one that claims every choice is optimal.
Which of your decisions would you reverse if Walt Brannigan were replaced in June? If the answer is “none”, check again.

prompts: Which four to six decisions are most vulnerable, and what is the best case against each?
Where do you concede, and how will you monitor that weakness?
What would change your mind on each decision?
Record each decision and confidence in the Strategic Decision Journal with a review date.

brief.text: Build the Department of Advance and Strategic Coordination for the Port Calder Lamplighters (fictional). You start as the only position. Add positions from the role menu, assign the in-season weekly work to them, and assign decision roles (Recommend, Decide, Input, Informed). All costs and hours are synthetic (Exhibit 3).

The base personnel envelope is $1,150,000 including your own position. The work list totals about 324 hours a week; you will not cover everything well. Decide what goes unassigned, what is bought from another department, and what you defer, and explain it in your narrative. Seasonal fellows or contractors funded from the investment fund are not positions here.
The Builder’s checks are transparent rules, not judgments of quality: a chart that passes every check can still fail politically, and one that fails a check can be right if you can explain why.

work.label: Defensive positioning cards and roster-change updates
Video packaging and tagging for coaches and players
Pre-series meeting with the coaching staff (prepare and attend)
Daily game-strategy brief for the field manager
In-person advance coverage of upcoming opponents
Spanish-language player materials and one-on-one sessions
Data pipeline, access controls and audit logging
Research agenda and evaluation of the department’s impact
Player development integration (shared language, call-up preparation)
Coverage of players new to the league from abroad
Weekly strategic summary for the GM and president
Stakeholder feedback loop and incident review

decisions.label: In-game strategy (lineups, bullpen use, defensive alignment within the rules)
Content and format of the player-facing opponent report
Defensive positioning recommendations for a series
Which player data the department may access and share
Hiring and assignment of department staff
Content of the weekly strategic summary to the GM and president

rules.text: The field manager decides in-game strategy (d1) under the scenario’s assumptions. If your chart gives the department “Decide” on d1 or d3, explain why the manager would accept it and what happens when he disagrees.
Data access (d4) is set by club policy with counsel. The department may Recommend or give Input; if you assign it “Decide”, explain how that is consistent with counsel’s request in the scenario.
Spanish-language work (w8) needs at least one position with the Spanish skill; one bilingual person covering all of it is a single point of failure across a 162-game season.
In-person coverage (w7) and international coverage (w12) involve travel; a position carrying either cannot also be the backup for the daily manager brief (w6).

Video work currently sits in the Video department and road scouts in Pro Scouting. Assigning w4 or w7 inside your department means proposing to move people or budget; address it in your decision rights and stakeholder components.
The loaned senior analyst leaves on May 31 and is not in the role menu. Any chart that relies on borrowed analysis must show who covers w1–w3 from June 1.

brief.text: Choose which of eight candidate investments to fund from the three-year strategic investment fund: $1,000,000 of Year 0 commitment authority (Exhibit 2). Cash flows are synthetic: Year 0 is the up-front outlay; Years 1–3 are net benefits after recurring costs.

Benefits combine two very different things: hard savings (analyst and video hours at finance’s $60 per hour, avoided fees and travel) and estimated run value at finance’s contested convention of $350,000 per run. Each project’s notes show the split. Scenario multipliers apply to benefits only. Several projects interact: the vendor platform (p1) and in-house pipeline (p2) largely substitute for each other, and the governance program (p4) may be required by counsel regardless of its NPV.
This is a teaching model of capital budgeting, not a forecast of what any department is worth.

projects.label: Vendor opponent-analytics platform (Exhibit 5, option A)
projects.description: Licensed platform with coach-facing views, running by spring training.
projects.notes: Year 0 = setup and first license year. Benefits net of a $140,000 annual license: about 1,700 analyst hours a year saved (≈ $100,000) plus an assumed 0.65–0.85 runs a year from faster, cleaner briefs. Roughly two thirds of the benefit is run value.
projects.nonfinancial: Rivals use the same tool; license limits on sharing; exit costs and data-export rights need counsel’s review.

projects.label: In-house pipeline built with Research and Analytics (option B)
projects.description: Club-owned data pipeline and models, fully ready around July.
projects.notes: Year 0 = engineering time and infrastructure. Benefits net of $90,000 maintenance; small in Year 1 because the pipeline is late, larger later as tailored models mature. Mostly run value; highly uncertain.
projects.nonfinancial: Club owns the code and models (a resource rivals cannot buy); depends on another department; key-person risk. Largely duplicates p1.

projects.label: Secure delivery: managed tablets, access tiers, logging (option C)
projects.description: Devices and software that control who sees which report.
projects.notes: Benefits = printing and distribution time saved plus expected loss avoided from license breaches and data incidents (probability × cost, both assumed).
projects.nonfinancial: Directly addresses the July and September incidents in Exhibit 6; supports trust of players and counsel.

projects.label: Data governance program (policy, inventory, training, privacy review)
projects.description: Written data-access policy, data inventory, staff training and an external privacy review.
projects.notes: Benefits are only avoided costs of incidents and rework, conservatively estimated; no run value assumed.
projects.nonfinancial: May be required by counsel and the collective bargaining agreement; protects health data and minors’ data. A negative NPV is not a reason to skip a legal obligation.

projects.label: Research fellowship and impact evaluation (two seasonal fellows a year)
projects.description: Contracted seasonal researchers who run pre-specified evaluations of the department’s practices.
projects.notes: Back-loaded: value arises only if evaluations identify practices worth keeping or stopping. Almost entirely run value; widest uncertainty of any project.
projects.nonfinancial: Builds the evidence the department needs to justify Year 2 growth; fellows are contractors, not Builder positions; intellectual-property terms needed.

projects.label: Contracted coverage of players from foreign leagues
projects.description: Part-time contract scouts in two foreign leagues plus translation, coordinated with International Scouting.
projects.notes: Benefits = run value from better preparation for about eleven players new to the league, plus travel avoided by staff scouts.
projects.nonfinancial: Requires agreement with the international scouting director; contractor confidentiality terms; respects her signing calendar.

projects.label: Coach co-design and bilingual education program
projects.description: Spring-training workshops, embedded sessions and bilingual materials co-designed with coaches.
projects.notes: Benefits assume higher use of recommendations (more of the department’s work is acted on), valued in runs; small and uncertain.
projects.nonfinancial: Addresses the coaches’ usability ratings and algorithm-aversion risk; signals respect for the bench coach’s role.

projects.label: Automated video tagging (Exhibit 5 add-on)
projects.description: Software that tags and indexes video automatically.
projects.notes: Benefits net of $60,000 a year: mostly video hours saved (hard savings) and faster clip delivery; accuracy for foreign-league video unknown.
projects.nonfinancial: Could reduce the need to move a video coordinator from the Video department, easing turf conflict.

questions: Which portfolio maximizes NPV within the fund, and does it include the governance program? What do you do about that?
Rank the projects by NPV, IRR and profitability index. Where do the rankings disagree, and which ranking should guide a budget-constrained choice?
Set the scenario to low. Which projects remain positive, and what do they have in common?
Suppose finance halves the run-value convention. Which projects’ cases collapse, and which survive on hard savings?
What does choosing p1 versus p2 say about your view of competitive advantage and of your relationship with Research and Analytics?

key.insights: At 8%, the NPV-maximizing portfolio within $1,000,000 funds the vendor platform, secure delivery, the research fellowship, foreign-league coverage and the coach program (about $960,000 of outlay), and leaves out data governance, whose NPV is slightly negative, and the in-house pipeline. A careful analyst notices three things. First, governance may be a legal requirement, in which case it is a constraint, not a candidate; funding it forces a swap, typically dropping or shrinking foreign-league coverage or secure delivery. Second, the projects with the highest IRR and profitability index (the coach program and the fellowship) are small and the most uncertain; in the low scenario the fellowship’s NPV falls sharply, while secure delivery and video tagging, which rest more on hard savings, hold up better. Third, the vendor platform beats the in-house pipeline on NPV mainly because it delivers value earlier; the pipeline’s case rests on ownership and later-year run value, which the cash flows only partly capture. Halving the run-value convention exposes how much of every case depends on one contested number.

scenario.text: Draft your speaker notes for the January 20 decision presentation to the president of baseball operations and the general manager of the Port Calder Lamplighters (fictional). You have forty minutes; plan to speak for about ten and leave the rest for questions.

audience.who: Miriam Castellanos, president of baseball operations
audience.cares: A plan she can defend to ownership; no war between departments; honest risks.
Connection to roster decisions; cost; what changes on the field and when.

checklist: Recommendation and decisions requested in the first two sentences
Each slide title is a full-sentence claim
Cost and first-year milestones stated with numbers
Top three risks and what you will not do are named
No promise of wins or runs
Ends with the specific decisions you need

milestones.text: Read the scenario and exhibits. Build a first chart in the Organization Builder and draft k03 structure, k04 staffing and k05 decision rights.
Draft k01 mission and vision, k02 strategic priorities and k08 stakeholder engagement; revise the Week 8 chart so structure follows strategy.
Run the Capital Allocation Lab and draft k06 budget, k07 technology and k12 research and evidence standards.
Draft k09 legal and ethical considerations (issues for counsel, not conclusions) and k10 organizational communication.
Draft k11 indicators, k13 change management and k14 the first 90 days; assemble the roadmap deliverable.
Run a premortem; draft k15 roadmap and k16 risk register and scenarios; revisit k09 with Week 13’s ethics and governance lens; assemble the strategic memo and budget model.

Draft k17 presentation in the Communication Studio and k18 written defense; write the executive summary and reflection; self-assess each deliverable against its rubric and log key decisions in the Decision Journal.

defense: Why should ownership fund a new department when you cannot show it will change a single game result this year?
You are spending most of the investment fund on things whose value depends on finance’s run-value convention. What is your plan if that number is half as large?
Walt Brannigan told you not to tell him how to run his bullpen. What, specifically, will your department do the first time he ignores a recommendation and loses the game?
Why did you not simply give Sanjay Mehra the budget and let Research and Analytics run Advance?
You took road scouts or video staff from other departments, or you did not. Either way, defend the choice to the department head who loses out.
What happens on June 1, when the loaned analyst leaves, if your hires have not worked out?
Counsel says no player health data in advance reports. The pitching coach says she cannot prepare without readiness information. Who wins, and how?
Why buy a platform that our rivals also use, or why build one that will not be ready until July?
Which of your indicators could your own staff game, and how would I know?
What did you decide not to do, and who will be unhappy about it?
If I cut your Year 1 budget by fifteen percent tomorrow, what goes first, and why that?
What evidence in October would lead you to recommend shrinking the department you are asking me to create?

audit.title: Research audit: reference programs and open resources behind APERTURE Semester I
audit.disclaimer: APERTURE is an independent, self-directed learning experience. It has no affiliation with, endorsement by, accreditation from, or partnership with any university or school named in this audit, and completing it earns no academic credit or degree. The programs below are programs whose public curricula informed this course; descriptions summarize public web pages as seen in search results on 2026-11-01 and may not reflect current requirements.

method.text: This audit examined fifteen reference programs in three cohorts of five: PhD programs in organizational behavior and behavioral science, MBA programs, and joint JD/MBA programs. The cohorts and starting institutions were chosen by the owner of APERTURE as a reference set. The audit does not rank them and makes no claim that they are the “top five” in any category; no ranking methodology was applied, and other strong programs (for example at Yale, Princeton, Columbia, MIT, Duke and elsewhere) could have served.

For each program the audit searched the official domains of the school (for example hbs.edu, gsb.stanford.edu, wharton.upenn.edu, mitsloan.mit.edu, chicagobooth.edu, kellogg.northwestern.edu, law.upenn.edu, hls.harvard.edu and university catalogs) for program pages, degree requirements, handbooks and course descriptions. The owner’s official starting URLs were used for the ten PhD and JD/MBA programs; official curriculum URLs for the five MBA programs were taken from search results on those schools’ domains.

**Environment limitation.** Pages could not be opened from the build environment: direct fetches failed, so every statement rests on the titles and text excerpts that web search returned on 2026-11-01. Each program therefore carries a verification record with its link marked “not-opened” and a note on which fields matched on which domain. Where search results disagreed (for example unit counts in different handbook years), the audit reports the disagreement instead of choosing silently. Programs whose key requirements rested on dated or ambiguous documents are marked partially confirmed.

The audit recorded, per program, what public pages confirm about core areas, required or first-year core courses, research-methods training and distinctive features, then mapped each program to the APERTURE weeks it informed. Public program pages describe structures and course titles, not full syllabi, so no claim is made about the week-by-week content of any course. The search budget available to the audit ran out before every candidate open resource could be checked; resources that could not be confirmed are omitted and listed under gaps.

criteria.label: Curricular transparency
criteria.description: The program publishes enough about its required courses, methods training and milestones on official pages to be described without guessing.

criteria.label: Disciplinary coverage
criteria.description: Together the programs span the three APERTURE schools — behavioral and social science, business and leadership, law and strategy — and each program adds something the others lack.

criteria.label: Research orientation and methodological rigor
criteria.description: The program trains students to evaluate or produce evidence (statistics, experimental and non-experimental design, research papers), which supports APERTURE’s evidence discipline.

criteria.label: Relevance to the learner’s objectives
criteria.description: The curriculum addresses executive breadth the learner wants: judgment, motivation, leadership, organizations, strategy, finance, negotiation, law and ethics.

criteria.label: Practical application
criteria.description: The program shows how knowledge is turned into decisions — cases, simulations, field work, capstones — which informs APERTURE’s exercises and cases.

criteria.label: Availability of open companion material
criteria.description: Related open educational resources exist (MIT OpenCourseWare, Open Yale Courses, OpenStax) so the learner can go deeper without paywalls.

programs.name: PhD in Organizational Behavior
programs.institution: Harvard Business School with the Harvard Kenneth C. Griffin Graduate School of Arts and Sciences

verified.evidence: Program name, URL and the micro/macro track structure matched on hbs.edu (program and program-requirements pages); joint administration with Harvard Griffin GSAS and the sociology link matched on gsas.harvard.edu and sociology.fas.harvard.edu.

programs.summary: A doctoral program, offered jointly by HBS and Harvard’s Griffin GSAS, that trains scholars to use the concepts and methods of psychology and sociology to study behavior and management in organizations. Students follow a micro (psychology-oriented) or macro (sociology-oriented) track; coursework and a field examination occupy roughly the first two years, followed by a research apprenticeship, a qualifying paper, a field research requirement, teaching and a dissertation typically made of three papers.
coreAreas: Micro organizational behavior (individual and group behavior, psychology-based)
Macro organizational behavior (organizations and institutions, sociology-based)
methods: Psychology and sociology research methods
Research apprenticeship (about 100 hours by end of year two)
Qualifying paper by end of year three
Field research requirement
programs.distinctive: Explicit two-discipline design (psychology and sociology) with course access across Harvard schools and MIT, and a required field research component tying theory to real organizations.
programs.howUsed: Its micro/macro split shaped APERTURE’s decision to teach behavior at three levels — individual judgment and motivation (Weeks 1–2), social systems and power (Week 6) and organizational design (Week 8) — and its apprenticeship and field-research requirements informed the applied, evidence-graded assignments of Week 4.
programs.limitations: Public pages describe milestones and tracks, not a full required-course list or syllabi; course choices are approved individually each semester, so no fixed core reading list could be confirmed. Requirements may differ by entering year.

programs.name: PhD in Organizational Behavior

verified.evidence: Field name, URL, micro and macro subareas, topics and track requirements (course numbers OB 654, OB 670, OB 675, OB 678, PSYCH 252) matched on gsb.stanford.edu field and track-requirement pages.

programs.summary: A doctoral field split into Micro OB, which draws mainly on psychology (cognition and decision-making, moral judgment, negotiation and bargaining, leadership, personality), and Macro OB, which trains researchers in organization theory and economic sociology (organizational culture, social networks and diffusion, labor-market inequality). Both tracks take a first-year proseminar and a field exam; the micro track requires statistics, micro research methods and a recurring experimental-research design course, while the macro track requires a research-design course, core theory courses and an econometrics or methods sequence.
methods: PSYCH 252 Statistical Methods for Behavioral and Social Sciences
OB 675 Micro Research Methods
OB 678 Design and Process of Experimental Research (each year, years 1–3, micro track)
OB 670 Designing Social Research (macro track)
Econometrics or methods sequence (macro track)
programs.distinctive: Unusually explicit, repeated training in experimental design for micro students, and a topical list that spans judgment, ethics, negotiation and networks — almost the full behavioral spine of APERTURE.
programs.howUsed: Its micro topics set the scope of Weeks 1, 2, 5 and 7 (judgment, motivation, leadership, negotiation) and its macro topics the network and culture content of Week 6; its methods sequence is the model for Week 4’s emphasis on design before statistics, and moral judgment informs Week 13.
programs.limitations: Track pages list course numbers and requirements but not syllabi or reading lists; field-exam timing differs between pages. Specific weekly content of the courses could not be confirmed.

programs.name: PhD in Management (organizational behavior, organization theory and strategy specializations)
programs.institution: The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania

verified.evidence: Program name, URL and specializations (Entrepreneurship, Human and Social Capital, Multinational Management, Organizational Behavior, Organizational Theory, Strategy) matched on doctoral.wharton.upenn.edu; required foundations and elective seminars matched on catalog.upenn.edu; milestones matched on the department handbook (mgmt.wharton.upenn.edu / doctoral-inside.wharton.upenn.edu).

programs.summary: A flexible, interdisciplinary management doctorate with six specializations. The university catalog lists required foundations in Economic Foundations of Management, Psychological Foundations of Research in Management, Foundations of Organizational Theory and a Seminar in Research Design, plus a methods sequence and specialization electives such as Seminar in Corporate Strategy, Seminar in Strategy and Organization Design, Technology and Innovation Strategy, Non-Market Strategy, Seminar in Macro-Organizational Behavior and Applied Research Methods in OB. Students sit a second-year qualifying exam and defend a second-year paper.
methods: Seminar in Research Design
Statistics sequence and additional research-methods units
Applied Research Methods in OB (elective)
Second-year paper and qualifying exam
programs.distinctive: The only PhD in the set that joins behavioral, sociological and economic foundations with formal strategy seminars, which makes it the bridge between APERTURE’s behavioral and business schools.
programs.howUsed: Its three foundations (economic, psychological, organizational) mirror APERTURE’s three-school design; its strategy and organization-design seminars informed Weeks 8–9 and its innovation and non-market strategy topics Week 12’s treatment of technology adoption.
programs.limitations: Unit counts differ between the catalog and handbook versions found; seminar syllabi were not available in search results, so content is inferred from course titles only.

programs.name: PhD in Management & Organizations
programs.institution: Kellogg School of Management, Northwestern University

verified.evidence: Program name, URL, first-year structure (nine courses, psychology and sociology foundations) and milestones matched on kellogg.northwestern.edu and catalogs.northwestern.edu. Exam and candidacy details come from a 2020 program-guidelines PDF on kellogg.northwestern.edu and may be out of date; a full current course list was not found.

programs.summary: A doctorate that, per the Northwestern catalog, integrates psychological, sociological, economic and complex-systems perspectives on organizations. First-year students take nine courses that give a broad theoretical grounding in psychology and sociology; a preliminary exam after year one covers four substantive core courses and two core methods courses. Students give research talks in years two and three, write an empirical candidacy paper and serve as research or teaching assistants. A separate joint program with Sociology exists.
coreAreas: Psychology of individuals and groups in organizations
methods: Two core methods courses (covered by the preliminary exam)
Macro-organizational research methods (joint sociology track)
Empirical candidacy paper
programs.distinctive: Explicit inclusion of complex-systems thinking alongside psychology and sociology.
programs.howUsed: Its complex-systems perspective informed the systems-thinking, feedback-loop and unintended-consequence material in Weeks 8 and 12; its psychology-plus-sociology first year reinforced the pairing of motivation (Week 2) with power and networks (Week 6).
programs.limitations: Only a partial course list was found (two macro course titles in the joint sociology program); the most detailed requirements came from a 2020 guideline document. Micro course titles and syllabi could not be confirmed.

programs.name: PhD in Behavioral Science
programs.institution: University of Chicago Booth School of Business

verified.evidence: Program name, URL, disciplinary basis (cognitive and social psychology, economics), joint Psychology and Business PhD and the Roman Family Center for Decision Research link matched on chicagobooth.edu. Course and exam requirements come from a Booth PhD guidebook whose current version could not be confirmed.

programs.summary: A Booth dissertation area whose research draws on theory and methods from cognitive and social psychology, economics and related fields, closely tied to the Roman Family Center for Decision Research, which studies decision making in individual, interpersonal, organizational, consumer and legal settings. Per the program guidebook, students take topical proseminars and research-methods courses (at least one experimental and one non-experimental), sit a second-year qualifying exam with a research report, write a curriculum paper and complete a dissertation. A joint PhD with the Department of Psychology is available.
methods: At least one experimental methods course
At least one non-experimental methods course
Second-year qualifying exam with research report
Curriculum paper
programs.distinctive: The set’s purest decision-science program: the research center’s scope (individual through legal decisions) runs across all three APERTURE schools.
programs.howUsed: It is the primary model for Week 1 (judgment, calibration, biases) and for the decision-under-uncertainty thread in Weeks 7 and 13; its requirement of both experimental and non-experimental methods shaped Week 4’s balance between randomized and observational designs; its cognitive-psychology basis supports the memory and retrieval material in Week 3.
programs.limitations: Requirements were confirmed only through guidebook excerpts of uncertain date; proseminar topics and syllabi were not visible. Admission and current course details should be checked with the program office.

programs.name: MBA Program (Required Curriculum, FIELD and Elective Curriculum)

verified.evidence: Curriculum page URL, Required Curriculum courses by term (Class of 2028), 30 elective credits, FIELD and the case method matched on hbs.edu (curriculum page, MBA handbook section 2.4 and 2.7, case-method page, faculty curriculum pages).

programs.summary: All first-year students take the same Required Curriculum and FIELD. Term 1: Finance 1, Financial Reporting and Control, Leadership and Organizational Behavior (LEAD), Marketing, Strategy, and Technology and Operations Management. Term 2: Business, Government and the International Economy; Data Science and AI for Leaders; The Entrepreneurial Manager; Finance 2; Leadership and Corporate Accountability; and Purpose of the Firm. Students then take the equivalent of 30 elective credits. Teaching relies on the case method: students read about 500 cases, each ending in a decision.
coreAreas: Business, government and the international economy
Data science and AI for leaders
methods: Data Science and AI for Leaders (required)
Case method (decision-forcing discussion)
FIELD (year-long experiential course with a Global Capstone)
programs.distinctive: Decision-forcing cases as the dominant pedagogy, a required course on corporate accountability and the firm’s purpose, and LEAD’s arc from team culture to organizational design to career strategy.
programs.howUsed: Its case method is the model for APERTURE’s weekly original cases with incomplete information and more than one defensible answer; LEAD informed Weeks 5 and 8, Finance 1–2 and Financial Reporting Week 10, Strategy Week 9, TOM Week 12, Leadership and Corporate Accountability and Data Science and AI for Leaders Week 13, and FIELD’s capstone the incremental Week 14 capstone; LEAD and FIELD’s learning-by-doing design also informed Week 3.
programs.limitations: Course descriptions were available for LEAD, Finance 1 and FIELD only; the Strategy course description and all syllabi were not visible. HBS cases are proprietary and are not used or reproduced; APERTURE writes its own cases.

programs.name: MBA Program (first-year curriculum)

verified.evidence: First-year page URL, the Analytical, Leadership and Management Foundations structure and course descriptions (data analysis, finance, financial accounting, microeconomics, optimization and simulation modeling, Leadership Foundations, Ethics, Managing Groups and Teams, Organizational Behavior, Leadership Labs, Executive Challenge) matched on gsb.stanford.edu.

programs.summary: The first-year core is divided into Analytical Foundations (data analysis, finance, financial accounting, microeconomics, optimization and simulation modeling), Leadership Foundations (a course on what kind of leader to be, taught in five-to-six-person squads, plus Ethics, Managing Groups and Teams, and Organizational Behavior) and Management Foundations (marketing, operations, general management and strategy, non-market strategy), with a choice among categories. Leadership Labs, a required autumn course, has squads practice through simulations and culminates in the Executive Challenge, a day of role-played business cases judged by alumni.
methods: Data analysis for inference and decisions
Optimization and simulation modeling
Simulation-based leadership practice with structured reflection
programs.distinctive: Leadership taught as deliberate practice in small squads with simulations and feedback, and a required ethics course grounded in research on human behavior.
programs.howUsed: Leadership Labs and the Executive Challenge are the model for APERTURE’s simulators and branching conversations (Week 5) and the capstone defense (Week 14); the Ethics course’s use of behavioral research informed Week 13; Analytical Foundations informed Weeks 4 and 10; non-market strategy informed Week 9; Organizational Behavior and Managing Groups and Teams informed Week 2; the practice-and-reflection design of Leadership Labs informed Week 3; the operations foundation informed Week 12.
programs.limitations: No single current numbered list of required courses was found; older lists are dated. Syllabi and readings were not visible.

programs.name: MBA Program (fixed and flexible core)
programs.institution: The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania

verified.evidence: Curriculum URL, fixed core (MGMT 6100 Foundations of Teamwork and Leadership; MKTG 6110; BEPP 6110/6120 microeconomics; STAT 6130/6210; WHCP 6160 or 6180) and flexible core (accounting, corporate finance FNCE 6110/6210, macroeconomics, legal studies and business ethics LGST 6110/6120/6130, operations) matched on mba.wharton.upenn.edu and mba-inside.wharton.upenn.edu core-curriculum pages and guides.

programs.summary: The core has a fixed portion taken with one’s cohort in the first fall — Foundations of Teamwork and Leadership, Marketing Management, microeconomics, statistics and a management or entrepreneurial communication course — and a flexible portion taken any time: accounting, corporate finance, macroeconomics, legal studies and business ethics, operations and further management and marketing options. A writing requirement also applies.
methods: Statistics core (STAT 6130 or 6210)
Operations and analytics options (for example Business Analytics)
programs.distinctive: A required legal-studies and business-ethics component inside the MBA core and a dedicated communication requirement with persuasive-writing options.
programs.howUsed: Its communication core informed Week 5’s three-format writing assignment (memo, brief, verbal); its legal-studies-and-ethics requirement supported placing law and ethics (Weeks 11 and 13) inside a general-management semester; statistics and operations informed Weeks 4 and 12; accounting and finance informed Week 10.
programs.limitations: Course numbers and credit values change by class year; negotiation appears in older core documents but could not be confirmed as part of the current core. Syllabi were not visible.

programs.name: MBA Program (first-semester core)

verified.evidence: Curriculum URL and the core structure (six required courses, one core elective, optional proseminar) matched on mitsloan.mit.edu and mbapolicyhandbook.mit.edu; Data, Models and Decisions (15.060) and Organizational Processes (15.311) descriptions and 15.002 Leadership Challenges for an Inclusive World matched on official MIT pages. The remaining course names (Economic Analysis, Communication for Leaders, Financial Accounting) appeared in MIT search-result text but a complete official list was not shown in one place.

programs.summary: The first semester (the Core) has six required courses, one core elective (for example Managerial Finance, 15.401) and an optional certificate proseminar. Required courses include Data, Models and Decisions (probability, decision analysis, statistics, regression, simulation and optimization), Organizational Processes (organizations seen through strategic-design, political and cultural lenses, with a team project), Economic Analysis, Communication for Leaders, Financial Accounting, and Leadership Challenges for an Inclusive World. MIT OpenCourseWare publishes a collection of first-semester core materials.
coreAreas: Organizational processes (design, political and cultural lenses)

synthesis.text: Read together, the fifteen programs agree on more than their marketing suggests. The five doctoral programs share a two- or three-discipline foundation: psychology for individual judgment, motivation and group behavior; sociology for networks, institutions and culture; and, at Wharton and Booth, economics for incentives and decisions. Every one of them front-loads research-methods training — Stanford’s micro track repeats an experimental-design course for three years, Booth requires both experimental and non-experimental methods, Wharton requires a research-design seminar and Kellogg examines two core methods courses after year one. The message is that behavioral knowledge is only as good as the evidence behind it.

The five MBA programs converge on a recognizable core: financial accounting and corporate finance, microeconomics, statistics or data analysis, strategy, operations, marketing, and leadership and organizational behavior. Several cores also reach beyond the classic functions. HBS now requires Data Science and AI for Leaders, Leadership and Corporate Accountability, and Purpose of the Firm; Stanford requires Ethics and practices leadership through simulations in Leadership Labs; Wharton puts legal studies and business ethics and a communication course in its core; MIT Sloan teaches organizations through strategic-design, political and cultural lenses; Booth’s single required course, LEAD, joins negotiation with interpersonal communication. Leadership, in other words, is taught as a skill that requires practice and feedback, and accountability and ethics are treated as core, not elective.

The JD/MBA programs add a layer of institutional literacy. Their law cores (contracts, torts, property, legislation and regulation, civil procedure, constitutional law) and professional-responsibility requirements teach how rules allocate risk and constrain organizations. Their distinctive features are integrative: Harvard’s joint seminar, Penn’s transaction capstone following one company from formation to restructuring, and the compressed three-year designs at Penn, Northwestern and Chicago, which force business foundations to be learned quickly and used at once.

APERTURE’s fourteen weeks reflect this shared structure. Weeks 1–4 correspond to the doctoral foundations: judgment and decision science (the Booth and Stanford micro model), motivation and social behavior, learning, and a research-literacy week built on the methods emphasis common to all five PhD programs. Weeks 5–8 correspond to the MBA leadership and organization cores, with negotiation placed in Week 7 as Booth, Stanford’s micro OB topics and the MIT negotiation course suggest. Weeks 9–10 correspond to the strategy and finance cores, Week 11 to the first-year law curriculum read for legal literacy, Weeks 12–13 to operations, governance and accountability, and Week 14 to the capstones and integrative experiences that HBS, Stanford, Penn and Harvard’s joint program use.

APERTURE also departs from these programs on purpose. It is a self-directed program for a single learner and grants no credit, degree or credential. It does not train researchers: it teaches the learner to judge evidence, not to produce publishable studies, so methods are compressed into one week and then applied throughout. It does not train lawyers: Week 11 aims at issue spotting and knowing when to call counsel, and it is labelled as general education, not legal advice. It replaces proprietary cases and course packs with original cases built on fictional organizations and synthetic data, and it links open resources rather than reproducing copyrighted materials. Finally, it grades the evidence behind every major claim and names replication failures, which program pages — written to describe programs, not to evaluate findings — do not do. The reference programs set the breadth; APERTURE’s own standards set the depth and the honesty of the evidence.

mapping.how: Booth’s decision-research focus and Stanford’s micro-OB topic of cognition and decision-making set the content (heuristics, calibration, base rates); the psychology-based micro track at Harvard reinforced starting with individual judgment; MIT’s Data, Models and Decisions informed the probability and decision-analysis framing; Booth’s behavioral-science faculty group informed the managerial angle.

The psychological foundations shared by the PhD programs (motivation, social influence, group behavior) and the economic foundations at Wharton (incentives) shaped a week that joins social psychology with incentive design; Stanford’s Organizational Behavior and Managing Groups and Teams courses informed the managerial application.

No reference program teaches learning science or motor learning directly; the week draws on the practice-and-feedback design of Stanford’s Leadership Labs and HBS’s LEAD and FIELD, and on the cognitive-psychology basis of Booth’s program, with Open Yale PSYC 110 as the open foundation. Most content rests on the research literature rather than program pages.

Every PhD program’s methods core (experimental and non-experimental design, research-design seminars, statistics sequences, Harvard’s research apprenticeship and field-research requirement) set the scope; MIT’s Data, Models and Decisions, HBS’s Data Science and AI for Leaders, Stanford’s data-analysis core and the Wharton and Booth statistics requirements set the executive level of the treatment.

Leadership cores (HBS LEAD, Stanford Leadership Foundations and Leadership Labs, Wharton Foundations of Teamwork and Leadership, Booth LEAD) and communication requirements (Wharton management communication, MIT Communication for Leaders) shaped the coaching, feedback and three-format writing work; Stanford’s micro-OB leadership topic informed the evidence review of leadership theories.

MIT’s political and cultural lenses and Booth’s Power and Influence course set the frame; the macro-OB and sociology tracks at Stanford, Harvard and Kellogg (networks, diffusion, institutions, culture) informed the network and legitimacy material.

Booth’s LEAD (negotiation with interpersonal communication) and Stanford’s micro-OB topic of negotiation and bargaining set the scope; Booth’s decision research informed anchoring and judgment in bargaining; the JD/MBA programs informed contractual commitments and principal-agent material; MIT OCW 15.667 is the open companion.

MIT’s strategic-design lens, HBS LEAD’s progression to organizational design, Wharton’s organization-theory and strategy-and-organization-design seminars and Kellogg’s complex-systems perspective informed structure, decision rights, coordination and systems thinking.

The MBA strategy cores (HBS Strategy, Stanford general management, strategy and non-market strategy, Booth’s strategy function) and Wharton’s doctoral strategy seminars (corporate, innovation, non-market) set the content; the economics-first foundations at Booth informed opportunity cost and trade-offs.

All five MBA cores require financial accounting and corporate finance (HBS Finance 1–2 and Financial Reporting and Control; Stanford finance and accounting; Wharton flexible core; MIT Financial Accounting and Managerial Finance option; Booth accounting foundation); the JD/MBA programs’ waivable finance and accounting cores informed the foundation-level entry point.

The first-year law cores (contracts, torts, legislation and regulation) set the legal-literacy scope; Penn’s transaction capstone informed reading provisions for business risk; Wharton’s legal-studies core supported teaching law to managers rather than lawyers.

Operations cores (HBS Technology and Operations Management, Stanford operations, Wharton operations options, Booth’s operations function) and Wharton’s technology-and-innovation strategy seminar informed implementation and technology adoption; Kellogg’s systems perspective informed feedback loops.

HBS’s Leadership and Corporate Accountability, Purpose of the Firm and Data Science and AI for Leaders, Stanford’s Ethics course, Wharton’s legal-studies and business-ethics requirement and the JD/MBA professional-responsibility requirements informed governance, accountability and data ethics; Stanford’s moral-judgment topic and Booth’s decision research informed ethical decision-making under uncertainty.

HBS’s FIELD Global Capstone, Stanford’s Executive Challenge, Penn’s JD/MBA Capstone, Harvard’s integrative joint seminar and MIT’s core team project informed an incremental, integrative capstone with a defended recommendation.

gaps.text: **Syllabi.** Public program pages describe structures, course titles and milestones, not syllabi, reading lists or weekly topics. No claim is made about what any course teaches week by week, and no course’s readings were used.

**Pages not opened.** Every statement rests on search-result excerpts from 2026-11-01. Several programs showed conflicting figures across handbook years (Wharton PhD unit counts, HLS/HBS pro bono hours, Northwestern law credits, Booth’s three-year eligibility, Stanford PhD field-exam timing); these are reported, not resolved.

**Incomplete course lists.** MIT Sloan’s full six-course core, Stanford GSB’s current numbered course list, Kellogg’s micro-track courses, Booth PhD proseminar topics and the course titles behind several Booth MBA category numbers could not be confirmed. Negotiation could not be confirmed as part of Wharton’s current MBA core.

**Thin coverage of learning science.** None of the reference programs teaches learning science, skill acquisition or motor learning as a core subject; Week 3 relies on the research literature rather than on program curricula.

**Open resources not yet confirmed.** The search budget ran out before OpenStax Business Law I Essentials, OpenStax Business Ethics, Open Yale ECON 159 Game Theory (only its title and address were seen), and MIT OpenCourseWare courses in behavioral economics and statistics could be verified. They are omitted rather than cited from memory and should be checked in a later session. The MIT OpenCourseWare collection of Sloan first-semester core materials was seen in search results but its publication details were not.

**Faculty publications.** The owner asked for faculty research to be considered; the audit did not attempt to characterize faculty publications at the program level, because doing so from search excerpts would risk misattribution. Faculty research enters APERTURE through the verified resource records of each week.

labs.name: Behavioral Decision Lab
labs.summary: Probability estimates, calibration, hypothetical outcomes and decisions under competing obligations.
labs.description: Practice the judgments that sit underneath every executive decision: how confident to be, how to weigh base rates against vivid stories, and how to act when obligations collide. Scores here are about calibration and reasoning, not about being right by luck.

labs.name: Negotiation Simulator
labs.summary: Multi-round, multi-issue bargaining against a rule-based counterpart with explicit assumptions.
labs.description: Negotiate packages across several issues against a counterpart whose behavior follows published rules. The debrief shows the value you created and claimed, the trades that mattered, and the deals you left on the table.

labs.name: Organizational Design Studio
labs.summary: Design incentives, practice systems, structures, stakeholder strategies and change sequences.
labs.description: Adjust responsibilities, reporting lines, staffing, incentives and budgets, and see which design risks each choice creates. Every effect is an ordinal teaching heuristic with its rationale and sources shown.

labs.name: Research Critique Lab
labs.summary: Simulate how sample size, selection, measurement and multiple testing distort what studies report.
labs.description: Run thousands of simulated studies to see sampling error, publication filters and undisclosed multiple testing at work, then apply the same skepticism to real research with the critique rubric.

labs.name: Financial Decision Studio
labs.summary: Budgets, discounted cash flows, capital rationing and strategic resource allocation.
labs.description: Compare investments by NPV, IRR, payback and profitability index under scenarios, find the opportunity cost of a portfolio, and test whether a resource allocation actually expresses a strategy.

labs.name: Executive Communication Studio
labs.summary: Difficult conversations, recommendations in three lengths, and decision presentations.
labs.description: Rehearse conversations where trust and clarity pull against each other, and draft recommendations against transparent text measures (length, speaking time, sentence load, hedging) and a self-check list. Content is never machine-graded.

labs.name: Contract Issue-Spotting Lab
labs.summary: Read fictional agreements clause by clause and flag commercial and legal risk.
labs.description: Practice legal-commercial reasoning on fictional documents: flag clauses, classify the risk, and compare your reading with an annotated key. Educational material about general legal concepts — not legal advice.

labs.name: Strategic Decision Journal
labs.summary: Structured records of consequential decisions, forecasts and later reviews.
labs.description: Record decisions before you know how they turn out: options, assumptions, what would change your mind and probability forecasts with resolve-by dates. Resolving forecasts later builds your personal calibration record.

library.title: Comparing meta-analyses and preregistered multiple-laboratory replication projects
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Not confirmed by search in this session: the shared web-search budget was exhausted after one query. Record written from well-established bibliographic knowledge (Nature Human Behaviour 2020 article); title, authors, year, venue and DOI must be re-checked before release.

library.summary: Compares meta-analyses with large preregistered multi-lab replications of the same psychological effects. Meta-analytic effect sizes were substantially larger, on average roughly three times the replication estimates, and bias-correction methods did not fully close the gap.
arguments: Meta-analyses of a biased literature inherit its bias.
Bias-adjustment methods help only partly.
Large preregistered replications are a better benchmark than meta-analyses of published studies.
library.design: Paired comparison of meta-analytic and multi-lab replication estimates for the same effects.
library.strengths: A direct test of meta-analysis against a strong benchmark.
library.limitations: Limited number of effect pairs; psychology only.
library.generalizability: Warns against treating any summary of published studies as the truth, in any field.
library.relevance: Why the top of the evidence pyramid can still be wrong.

library.title: Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
library.license: © AAAS. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Not confirmed by search in this session: the shared web-search budget was exhausted after one query. Record written from well-established bibliographic knowledge (Science 1974 article); title, authors, year, venue and DOI must be re-checked before release.

library.summary: The classic statement of the representativeness, availability and anchoring heuristics. In the section on representativeness it discusses misconceptions of regression, including flight instructors who concluded that criticism works better than praise.
arguments: People judge probability by resemblance and neglect base rates and sample size.
People fail to expect regression toward the mean and invent causal explanations for it.
Heuristics are useful but produce systematic, predictable errors.
library.design: Synthesis of the authors’ earlier experiments and illustrative problems.
library.strengths: Seminal, highly cited, clearly argued.
library.limitations: Many illustrations are vignette studies with student samples; later work debates how often these errors matter in natural environments.
library.contested: The ecological-rationality school argues some biases shrink with natural frequencies; the regression point itself is a statistical fact, not contested.
library.generalizability: The regression misconception transfers directly to coaching, performance review and turnaround management.
library.relevance: The source of the flight-instructor example used in Lesson 1.

library.title: Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced. A copy is posted on an MIT course page.

verified.evidence: Title, sole author, journal, volume 44 issue 2, pages 350–383 and DOI matched on dash.harvard.edu, citedrive.com and a journal index (acnpsearch); sample of 51 work teams in a manufacturing company and findings matched in the abstract; a PDF is listed on web.mit.edu.

library.summary: Introduces team psychological safety — a shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking — and studies it in 51 work teams of one manufacturing company. Psychological safety was associated with learning behavior, which in turn mediated its relationship with team performance; team efficacy was not associated with learning once safety was controlled.
arguments: Psychological safety is a team-level shared belief, not a personality trait.
It is associated with learning behaviors such as asking for help and discussing errors.
Learning behavior mediates the link between safety and team performance.
Team structures, including context support and team-leader coaching, shape safety.
library.design: Field study of 51 work teams in one manufacturing company measuring antecedent, process and outcome variables.
library.strengths: Defines the construct with care and tests a full antecedent–process–outcome model in real teams.
library.limitations: One company; largely cross-sectional, so the direction of causation cannot be established.
library.contested: The construct is well supported as a correlate of learning; causal claims rest on later work, summarized meta-analytically in R-frazier-2017-psychological.
library.generalizability: Broad across team-based work; the mechanism (speaking up) is plausible in medicine, aviation, software and coaching staffs, but effect sizes are not transferable.
library.relevance: The founding empirical paper for the idea; read it to see what it does and does not claim before you encounter its popular versions.

library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.method: writer-knowledge (web search unavailable: shared search budget exhausted)
verified.evidence: Not checked by web search in this session. Title, authors, year and venue (Perspectives on Psychological Science, 9(6), 641–651) entered from the writer's knowledge of this widely cited work; confirm against the DOI resolver or publisher before release.

library.title: Beyond Power Calculations: Assessing Type S (Sign) and Type M (Magnitude) Errors
library.summary: When studies are small and noisy, statistically significant estimates tend to exaggerate the true effect (type M error) and can have the wrong sign (type S error). The authors propose design analysis to estimate these risks.
arguments: Significance filtering in low-power settings inflates effect estimates.
Sign errors are possible when power is very low.
Design analysis should use realistic external effect-size assumptions.
library.design: Statistical argument with worked examples and simulation.
library.strengths: Directly relevant to small-sample operational analytics.
library.limitations: Requires a defensible prior estimate of the plausible effect size.
library.generalizability: High for evaluating whether advance work changed outcomes over a few dozen series.
library.relevance: Protects you from announcing that the department “saved 30 runs” on one season of noisy data.

library.title: Understanding and misunderstanding randomized controlled trials
library.license: Open access (Creative Commons license believed; not re-confirmed). Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Not confirmed by search in this session: the shared web-search budget was exhausted after one query. Record written from well-established bibliographic knowledge (Social Science & Medicine 2018 article); title, authors, year, venue and DOI must be re-checked before release.

library.summary: Argues that randomized trials are valuable but widely misunderstood. Randomization balances confounders only in expectation, estimates average effects that may hide heterogeneity, and says little by itself about whether a result will hold elsewhere.
arguments: A single trial does not guarantee balance in the sample actually drawn.
Average treatment effects can conceal people who are harmed.
Using a result elsewhere requires understanding why it worked.
library.strengths: Rigorous critique from an economist and a philosopher of science.
library.limitations: Some trialists argue it understates how RCT practice already addresses these concerns.
library.contested: Design-based economists defend randomized evidence as the most credible available (R-angrist-2010-credibility).
library.generalizability: Central for anyone importing results from another organization or league.
library.relevance: The strongest case for treating evidence hierarchies as a starting point, not a verdict.

library.title: An Excess of Positive Results: Comparing the Standard Psychology Literature With Registered Reports
library.publication: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 4(2)
library.license: Open access (license not re-confirmed). Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Not confirmed by search in this session: the shared web-search budget was exhausted after one query. Record written from well-established bibliographic knowledge (AMPPS 2021 article); title, authors, year, venue and DOI must be re-checked before release.

library.summary: Compares the share of supported first hypotheses in a sample of standard psychology papers with a sample of Registered Reports, in which journals accept the study before results are known. Positive results were far rarer among Registered Reports.
arguments: About 96% of standard reports supported their first hypothesis, against about 44% of Registered Reports.
The gap is consistent with publication bias and flexible analysis in the standard literature.
Registered Reports are a practical structural remedy.
library.design: Comparison of two samples of published articles coded for hypothesis support.
library.strengths: Simple, transparent comparison with an informative contrast group.
library.limitations: Registered Reports may test different, riskier hypotheses; the comparison is not randomized.
library.generalizability: Supports pre-commitment devices for internal studies: decide what counts as success before the data arrive.
library.relevance: Shows what the literature looks like when results cannot shape publication.

library.title: The Effects of Feedback Interventions on Performance: A Historical Review, a Meta-Analysis, and a Preliminary Feedback Intervention Theory
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Not confirmed in this session: the shared web-search budget was exhausted before this record could be searched. Metadata entered from the standard citation; check title, venue, pages and DOI before relying on it.

library.summary: A historical review and meta-analysis of feedback interventions. Feedback improved performance on average, but a large share of interventions reduced performance. The authors propose feedback intervention theory: feedback works by directing attention, and it helps less, or harms, when it draws attention away from the task toward the self.
arguments: Feedback interventions have a positive average effect but highly variable results.
A substantial share of feedback interventions lowered performance.
Feedback that directs attention to the self (praise or criticism of the person) tends to weaken effects; feedback about the task and how to improve it tends to help.
library.design: Meta-analysis of feedback-intervention studies with a control condition, plus a theoretical synthesis.
library.strengths: Seminal; the variability finding has shaped feedback research for three decades.
library.limitations: Many included studies were laboratory tasks; workplace coaching conversations are richer than the interventions coded.
library.generalizability: The attention mechanism is plausible across settings; precise effect sizes should not be transferred to managerial conversations.
library.relevance: The strongest single correction to the belief that more feedback is always better.
