library.summary: A meta-analysis of 128 laboratory experiments on whether rewards reduce people’s later, freely chosen engagement in an interesting task. The authors conclude that expected, tangible rewards made contingent on doing the task reliably undermine intrinsic motivation, while positive verbal feedback tends to enhance it. They interpret the pattern through cognitive evaluation theory: rewards experienced as controlling reduce felt autonomy; rewards experienced as information about competence do not.
arguments: Expected tangible rewards contingent on engagement, completion or performance undermine free-choice intrinsic motivation for interesting tasks.
Verbal rewards (positive feedback) tend to enhance intrinsic motivation, especially for adults.
Whether a reward is felt as controlling or as informational is the moderating mechanism.
The paper rebuts an earlier meta-analysis (Cameron & Pierce, 1994) that reached a more benign conclusion.
library.design: Meta-analysis of 128 experiments, mostly laboratory studies with student participants and interesting tasks.
library.strengths: Large, systematic synthesis; separates reward types and contingencies rather than asking whether “rewards” in general help or hurt.
library.limitations: Mostly short laboratory sessions with tasks chosen to be interesting; the outcome is minutes of free-choice play, not job performance. Generalization to paid work, where pay is expected and necessary, is indirect.
library.contested: Cameron, Pierce and colleagues disputed the coding and conclusions in a published exchange; the undermining effect’s size and scope in workplaces remains debated. Compare R-cerasoli-2014-intrinsic, which finds intrinsic motivation and incentives jointly predict performance.
library.generalizability: Moderate for leaders: the mechanism (controlling vs. informational rewards) transfers well; the effect size from lab play sessions should not be imported into compensation design.
library.relevance: The core evidence behind “rewards can backfire” — and the conditions that claim needs. Essential before designing recognition or bonus systems for people who already care about their craft.

Reciprocity helps enforce contracts and norms that cannot be written down fully.
Cooperation in groups tends to decay without the possibility of punishing free riders and can be sustained with it.
Explicit incentives perceived as hostile or distrustful can reduce reciprocal effort.

library.summary: Yukl and Tracey examined how the influence tactics managers use relate to the task commitment of the people they try to influence — subordinates, peers and bosses — and to ratings of the managers’ effectiveness. Ingratiation and exchange were moderately effective with subordinates and peers but not with superiors.
arguments: Influence tactics differ in how likely they are to produce commitment rather than compliance or resistance.
Rational persuasion, inspirational appeals and consultation are most associated with commitment.
Pressure, legitimating and coalition tactics are least associated with commitment.
The direction of influence matters: some tactics work downward or laterally but not upward.
library.design: Field questionnaire study in which targets (subordinates, peers, bosses) described managers’ influence behavior and their own commitment; correlational.
library.strengths: Uses target reports rather than only agents’ self-reports; covers all three directions of influence; built on a validated taxonomy of tactics.
library.limitations: Cross-sectional and correlational; tactic choice is endogenous (people use pressure when they already expect resistance); common-method concerns.
library.generalizability: Reasonable for Western organizational settings; tactic effectiveness may differ across cultures and relationships.
library.relevance: Evidence-based guidance on influencing your peers and your boss, not only your staff.

library.title: The Romance of Leadership

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, year, volume 30 issue 1, pages 78–102 and DOI 10.2307/2392813 matched on scilit.com; volume and pages matched in later citations (Durham repository memorial piece, Collinson et al. 2007). library.summary: Meindl and colleagues argue that people hold a romanticized view of leadership: they explain organizational outcomes by pointing to leaders, and they do so more strongly when outcomes are extreme. The paper reports several studies, consistent with that attributional bias. It reframes part of “leadership” as something observers construct after the fact.
arguments: Observers over-attribute organizational performance to leaders relative to other causes.
The tendency strengthens when outcomes are unusually good or unusually bad.
Leadership is partly a perception held by followers and observers, not only a property of the leader.
library.design: A set of empirical studies (a secondary description counts five); design details were not confirmed in search results.
library.strengths: Seminal, widely cited, and opens a falsifiable alternative explanation for why leaders receive credit and blame.
library.limitations: Older studies; shows that attributions are inflated, not that leaders have no effect.
library.contested: Not a replication controversy; the debate is about how large real leader effects are relative to attributions. Read alongside R-vanknippenberg-2013-critical, which argues that outcome-contaminated perceptions also distort leadership measures.
library.generalizability: High for any field where outcomes are noisy and visible (sports, markets, hospitals, politics). Treat as a strong caution, not a precise estimate.
library.relevance: Every evaluation of a manager, coach or executive in a high-variance environment is exposed to this bias, including your own reputation.

library.title: Selling Issues to Top Management
library.license: © Academy of Management. Linked, not reproduced.

library.summary: Dutton and Ashford argue that middle managers shape what top management pays attention to by “selling” issues — calling attention to trends, events and problems and framing them. They develop a framework drawing on three perspectives: issue selling as upward influence, as claiming behavior (asserting that an issue deserves attention), and as impression management, since sellers risk their image. The framework explains when managers will try to sell an issue and how the way they package it and the process they use affects success.
arguments: Top management’s agenda is shaped from below by the issues middle managers choose to raise.
Whether managers try to sell an issue depends on perceived chances of success and on image risk.
Success depends on how an issue is packaged (framing, bundling) and on the selling process (timing, channels, involvement of others).
Issue selling is a political act and an impression-management act at once.
library.design: Theoretical framework with propositions; later tested in field studies by the authors and colleagues.
library.strengths: Puts middle managers at the center of strategic change; generated a substantial empirical literature.
library.limitations: Propositions rather than tests; draws on U.S. corporate settings.
library.generalizability: Applies to anyone who needs senior attention for an issue they do not own — in firms, agencies, hospitals or sports organizations.
library.relevance: The core theory of managing upward when you want leaders to care about your issue.

library.title: Organization Design: An Information Processing View
library.summary: Galbraith treats organizational design as a problem of information processing: the more uncertain the task, the more information must flow during execution. Organizations either reduce the need for information (slack, self-contained units) or increase capacity to process it (vertical information systems, lateral relations such as liaison roles and integrators).
arguments: Task uncertainty drives the information-processing load a structure must carry.
Rules, hierarchy and goals handle routine coordination; exceptions overload them.
Design options either reduce information needs or increase processing capacity, and each has costs.
library.design: Conceptual framework built from organizational case experience.
library.strengths: Gives a concrete menu of coordination mechanisms and the logic for choosing among them.
library.limitations: Pre-dates modern information technology and networked organizations; not a tested predictive model.
library.generalizability: High for coordination-heavy units such as a department that links scouting, analytics, coaching and the front office.
library.relevance: A strategic coordination department is, by definition, a lateral information-processing mechanism; this explains when it is worth its cost.

library.title: The External Control of Organizations: A Resource Dependence Perspective
library.publication: Original edition 1978; reissued as a Stanford Business Classic by Stanford University Press, 2003 (with a new preface by Pfeffer)
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors and the 2003 Stanford University Press reissue (Stanford Business Classics, new preface by Pfeffer) matched on gsb.stanford.edu and sup.org; a 1978 original date appeared in a listing but the original publisher was not confirmed in search results, so it is not named here.

library.summary: Pfeffer and Salancik argue that organizations are best understood through their dependence on external actors who control resources they need. Because dependence creates the possibility of external control, much of what organizations do — co-opting outsiders onto boards, forming alliances, merging, diversifying suppliers — can be read as attempts to manage dependence. The same logic, building on power-dependence theory in sociology, explains power inside organizations: units that supply what others critically need, and cannot easily get elsewhere, gain influence.
arguments: An organization’s dependence on another actor grows with the importance of the resource, the other actor’s discretion over it, and the scarcity of alternatives.
Dependence creates the possibility of external control; organizations respond by managing or restructuring their dependencies.
Common responses include co-optation, alliances, mergers and diversification of resource sources.
Power is relational and situational: it shifts when critical contingencies shift.
library.design: Theoretical book synthesizing prior empirical work; tested extensively by later studies.
library.strengths: One of the foundational theories of organizations; turns power from a personality trait into a structural relation that can be mapped and changed.
library.limitations: Explains why actors gain influence better than how they use it; later reviews note that the theory was often invoked as a metaphor rather than tested directly.
library.contested: Broadly accepted as a perspective; individual predictions (for example about mergers or board co-optation) have mixed support. Institutional theory (R-dimaggio-1983-iron) offers a competing explanation of the same organizational behavior.
library.generalizability: High for any organization that depends on outside resources — public agencies, hospitals, firms and sports organizations alike.
library.relevance: The clearest way to answer “who actually has leverage here, and why?” before you try to change anything.

library.summary: A book for managers arguing that getting things done in organizations requires understanding and using power, and that discomfort with power leads capable people to fail at implementation. Pfeffer synthesizes research on the sources of power, including structural position and control of resources, together with extended organizational examples, and discusses the strategies and tactics through which power is used.
arguments: Implementation problems are largely problems of influence: mobilizing support and overcoming resistance.
Power comes substantially from structural position, control of resources and information, and alliances, not only from personal attributes.
Timing, framing and the management of interpersonal relations are tools for using power.
Managers who avoid power out of discomfort tend to lose to those who do not.
library.design: Practitioner synthesis by an organizational scholar; illustrative cases and narrative review, not a new empirical test.
library.strengths: Grounded in the author’s own academic research tradition; unsentimental about how organizations work; useful catalog of sources and tactics.

library.summary: A review showing that accountability improves judgment only under specific conditions: when people expect to justify themselves before they decide, to an audience whose views are unknown, who cares about accuracy and process. library.summary: Fifty years after his 1961 proof that the long-run average number of items in a queuing system equals the arrival rate multiplied by the average time each item spends in the system (L = λW), Little reviews how the result has been extended and used, with emphasis on practice in operations management and computing, and proves versions of the law for finite observation periods.
arguments: L = λW holds under very general conditions for long-run averages, without assumptions about arrival or service distributions.
In practice it links work-in-process, throughput and cycle time: knowing two gives the third.
Finite-period versions matter for managers, who observe real systems over limited windows.
library.design: Review and mathematical exposition, with proofs of finite-period versions.
library.strengths: Authoritative account by the law’s originator; bridges theory and practical use.
library.limitations: Mathematical; the law describes averages and says nothing by itself about variability or causes.
library.generalizability: Applies to any flow of work—patients, cases, tickets, contracts, player evaluations—when measured consistently over a stable period.
library.relevance: The single most useful equation for reasoning about backlogs and lead times in any operation you run.

library.summary: An essay with a simple model: the probability that a statistically significant finding is true depends on the prior odds that tested hypotheses are true, statistical power, and bias. Under realistic values in many fields, most claimed findings would be false.
arguments: Small studies, small effects, many tested relationships and flexible designs lower the chance a finding is true.
Financial interest and “hot” fields with many competing teams make it worse.
Significance alone says little; the prior and the power matter.
library.design: Analytic model of positive predictive value with illustrative scenarios.
library.strengths: Makes the base-rate logic of research explicit.
library.limitations: The title’s claim depends on assumed inputs; critics argue empirical false-discovery rates in some fields are lower.
library.contested: Some statisticians estimated lower false-discovery rates in medical literatures; the logical argument about priors and power is widely accepted.
library.generalizability: Directly applies to a portfolio of internal experiments: if most ideas tested are long shots, most “wins” are noise.
library.relevance: Connects Week 1 base rates to the reliability of research and analytics.

library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

library.summary: Kotter’s influential practitioner article lists eight errors he observed in corporate transformation efforts and, by implication, eight steps for leading change: establish urgency, form a guiding coalition, create a vision, communicate it, empower others to act, plan for short-term wins, consolidate gains, and institutionalize new approaches. It later became the basis of his book of the same name.
arguments: Transformation is a multi-phase process; skipping phases creates an illusion of speed.
Insufficient urgency and an under-powered guiding coalition are common early errors.
Visible short-term wins sustain commitment through a long change effort.
Changes are not secure until they are anchored in the organization’s norms and succession.
library.design: Experience-based synthesis from the author’s observation of corporate change efforts; no systematic data reported.
library.strengths: Clear, memorable sequence; directs attention to coalition and communication problems that analytical leaders often neglect.
library.limitations: Not empirically tested in the article; linear sequence; success and failure judged retrospectively by the author. Later empirical tests of the full model are limited.
library.contested: Widely used but weakly tested; its sequencing and universality are questioned by scholars, and the popular “70% of change fails” figure sometimes attached to it lacks a valid evidential base (see R-hughes-2011-do).
library.generalizability: Useful as a checklist in any organization; do not treat the order of steps or their completeness as validated.
library.relevance: The most common change model you will meet in boardrooms; you need to know it, use what is useful, and recognize what it does not prove.

library.title: The Bases of Social Power
library.publication: In D. Cartwright (Ed.), Studies in Social Power (pp. 150–167). Ann Arbor: Institute for Social Research, University of Michigan
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, editor, volume title, 1959 date, Ann Arbor publication and pages 150–167 matched on the Institute for Social Research site (cdn.isr.umich.edu), which hosts a digitized copy of the chapter and of the full volume; bibbase.org lists the same pages. Sources disagree on whether the publisher is styled the University of Michigan Press; the ISR copy was followed.

library.summary: French and Raven proposed that the power one person holds over another rests on a small number of distinct bases: reward, coercive, legitimate, referent and expert power. Each base is defined from the perspective of the person being influenced: power exists because the target believes the agent can reward, punish, rightfully direct, serve as a model of identification, or knows more. The chapter is a theoretical typology, not an empirical study.
arguments: Power is a relation between an agent and a target, located in the target’s perceptions, not a possession of the agent alone.
Five bases are distinguished: reward, coercive, legitimate, referent and expert.
Different bases have different side effects; coercion, for example, requires surveillance and tends to reduce attraction to the agent.
The range of a base differs: expert power, for instance, is limited to the domain in which the agent is seen as knowledgeable.
library.design: Conceptual typology drawing on the authors’ field theory tradition; no new data.
library.strengths: Simple, memorable and still the most widely used vocabulary for the sources of interpersonal power; defined from the target’s perspective, which keeps attention on perception.
library.limitations: The bases overlap (a boss’s legitimate power usually carries reward and coercive power with it); the typology is about interpersonal power and says little about structural sources such as control of resources or network position; later research measuring the bases has relied heavily on self-report questionnaires.
library.contested: Not contested as a vocabulary; its usefulness as a measurement framework is debated. Raven later added informational power as a further base. Structural accounts of power (R-pfeffer-1978-external) treat the bases as consequences of dependence rather than as primary.
library.generalizability: Transfers well as a diagnostic vocabulary for any organization, including sports organizations. It does not predict which base will work in a given setting.
library.relevance: Gives you the language to separate the authority your title grants from the power that colleagues actually attribute to you.

library.title: False-Positive Psychology: Undisclosed Flexibility in Data Collection and Analysis Allows Presenting Anything as Significant
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Not confirmed by search in this session: the shared web-search budget was exhausted after one query. Record written from well-established bibliographic knowledge (Psychological Science 2011 article); title, authors, year, venue and DOI must be re-checked before release.

library.summary: Using simulations and two deliberately absurd experiments, the authors show that common, individually defensible analytic choices can push the false-positive rate far above the nominal 5%. They propose disclosure requirements for authors and reviewers.
arguments: Choosing among dependent variables, adding observations after peeking, adding covariates and dropping conditions each inflate false positives.
Combined, these researcher degrees of freedom can produce a false-positive rate above 60% in their simulation.
Simple disclosure rules would make this flexibility visible.
library.design: Monte Carlo simulation plus two small demonstration experiments.
library.strengths: Clear mechanism, memorable demonstration, practical remedies.
library.limitations: Simulated rates depend on assumed combinations of choices; it does not estimate how often researchers actually do this.
library.generalizability: Applies to any dashboard or analysis where the analyst can choose metrics, windows, segments and stopping rules after seeing the data.
library.relevance: The cleanest explanation of why an honest analyst can still produce false findings.

library.title: Surprised by the Hot Hand Fallacy? A Truth in the Law of Small Numbers
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

library.summary: Shows that a standard way of measuring streak shooting is biased: in finite sequences, the proportion of successes following a run of successes is expected to be below the true rate. Correcting this bias reverses the classic conclusion that the hot hand in basketball is a fallacy.
arguments: Selecting outcomes that follow streaks within finite sequences creates a downward bias.
Reanalysis of the original controlled shooting data shows evidence of streak shooting.
A celebrated “bias” finding rested partly on a statistical artifact.
library.design: Mathematical proof plus reanalysis of controlled shooting data.
library.strengths: Rigorous; overturns a famous result through measurement logic.
library.limitations: Size and practical importance of the hot hand in games remains debated.
library.contested: The original hot-hand-fallacy research (Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky, 1985) concluded the opposite; debate continues about effect size in game conditions.
library.generalizability: Directly relevant to sports performance analysis and to any streak-based judgment.
library.relevance: Assignment option (sports performance).

library.license: Free to read from the American Economic Association (terms not re-confirmed). Linked, not reproduced.

library.summary: Argues that empirical economics became more credible because researchers focused on research design — randomized trials and natural experiments — rather than on elaborate models. Reviews how designs such as instrumental variables, regression discontinuity and differences-in-differences answer causal questions.
arguments: Design-based studies make the source of identifying variation explicit.
Randomized and quasi-experimental evidence has changed conclusions in labor, education and health economics.
Structural modeling and macroeconomics have been slower to adopt design-based standards.
library.strengths: Readable overview by two leading practitioners; free to read.
library.limitations: An advocate’s account; critics argue design-based studies answer narrow questions with limited external validity.
library.contested: Deaton and Cartwright, among others, argue the credibility gained comes at a cost in generalizability (R-deaton-2018-understanding).
library.generalizability: The design logic transfers to any organization evaluating its own programs.
library.relevance: The intellectual backbone of Lesson 3.

library.title: A Causal Test of the Strength of Weak Ties
library.license: © AAAS. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, five authors, journal, volume 377, issue 6612, pages 1304–1310 and DOI 10.1126/science.abl4476 matched on pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov and the Stanford Digital Economy Lab publication page; an author copy is posted on ide.mit.edu.

library.summary: Using multiple large-scale randomized experiments on LinkedIn’s “People You May Know” recommendation feature, which varied the kinds of connections offered to more than 20 million members, the authors provide a causal test of Granovetter’s weak-ties hypothesis for job mobility. They find an inverted-U relationship: moderately weak ties were most associated with job transmission, while the weakest and strongest ties were less helpful, and weak ties mattered more in more digital industries.
arguments: Experimental variation in network formation allows a causal estimate of the value of weak ties, which earlier observational work could not provide.
The relationship between tie strength and job mobility is nonlinear (inverted U), not “the weaker the better”.
The value of weak versus strong ties differs across industries.
library.design: Randomized experiments embedded in a platform’s connection-recommendation algorithm, analysed for downstream job transitions.
library.strengths: Very large scale; randomization addresses the selection problem that weakens most network studies; directly tests a classic theory.
library.limitations: One platform and one outcome (job mobility); tie strength is measured by structural proxies on an online network; raised public discussion about experimentation on platform users.
library.contested: Supports and refines R-granovetter-1973-strength rather than contradicting it.
library.generalizability: Strong for information-driven labor markets; inferences to influence inside a single organization are by analogy.
library.relevance: A model of how a famous idea can be tested causally — and of how the tested version turns out more nuanced than the slogan.

library.summary: Uses Oregon’s 2008 lottery for Medicaid slots to estimate the effects of coverage two years later. library.design: Randomized lottery with instrumental-variable estimates of the effect of coverage.

library.title: Fostering Implementation of Health Services Research Findings into Practice: A Consolidated Framework for Advancing Implementation Science
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

library.summary: The authors consolidate constructs from published implementation theories into the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR), organized in five domains: characteristics of the intervention, the outer setting, the inner setting, characteristics of the individuals involved, and the process of implementation. CFIR is a common vocabulary for diagnosing why an effective practice takes hold in one setting and not another, and for structuring evaluations across studies.
arguments: Effective interventions frequently fail to produce results when moved into new settings; context explains much of the difference.
Constructs from many theories can be merged into one structured menu covering five domains.
Interventions have core components and an adaptable periphery that can be tailored locally.
The framework is meant to guide formative evaluation and to accumulate knowledge across studies.
library.design: Review and synthesis of published implementation theories, with constructs selected for conceptual or empirical support and measurability.
library.strengths: Open access; widely adopted; gives a systematic checklist of contextual factors.
library.limitations: A determinant framework, not a predictive model; many constructs; developed in health services. The authors published an updated version in 2022.
library.generalizability: Designed for health care but used across education, social services and other sectors; works as a diagnostic structure for any multi-site rollout.
library.relevance: Gives you a disciplined way to separate what must stay constant in a rollout from what each site should adapt.

library.title: Psychological Safety: A Meta-Analytic Review and Extension
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.method: web-search (by the Week 5 writer in this build; cross-checked against that record)
verified.evidence: Not searched by this writer (search budget exhausted). The identical record in sources/w05.json reports title, five authors, journal, volume 70 issue 1, pages 113–165 and DOI matched on econbiz.de, zendy.io and university repositories; every field here matches that record.

library.summary: A meta-analysis of the psychological safety literature — the shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks such as asking questions or admitting errors. Psychological safety was associated with information sharing, learning behavior, engagement and performance, and was itself associated with supportive leadership and work design. Most of the underlying studies are correlational.
arguments: Psychological safety correlates positively with learning behavior, engagement and task performance.
Supportive leadership, peer support and work design characteristics are associated with higher psychological safety.
The construct operates at individual, team and organizational levels.
library.design: Meta-analysis of primarily cross-sectional field studies.
library.strengths: Aggregates a large field literature; examines antecedents and outcomes together.
library.limitations: Primary studies are mostly cross-sectional and often single-source, so causal direction and common-method bias are real concerns.
library.contested: Causal claims (“building psychological safety raises performance”) rest on thinner experimental and longitudinal evidence than popular accounts suggest.
library.generalizability: Relevant to any team that depends on speaking up about errors; sport-specific evidence is limited.
library.relevance: Separates the evidence on psychological safety from the slogan, so you can use the idea without overselling it.

library.title: Do 70 Per Cent of All Organizational Change Initiatives Really Fail?
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

The DOI was given in the search query and is consistent with the journal’s DOI pattern but was not shown on an authoritative page in the results.

library.summary: Hughes traces the widely repeated claim that about 70 per cent of organizational change initiatives fail to the published sources usually cited for it and concludes that there is no valid and reliable empirical evidence supporting the figure. Some of the sources concerned narrower programs such as business-process reengineering, and others offered the figure without a documented method.
arguments: The 70 per cent figure circulates as a narrative, not as a measured base rate.
The five sources examined do not provide valid and reliable evidence for a general failure rate of organizational change.
“Failure” is rarely defined, making any single rate across all change initiatives hard to measure.
Repeating the figure may itself shape how change is managed and justified.
library.design: Critical review tracing the evidence behind five frequently cited sources of the 70 per cent claim.
library.strengths: Goes back to primary sources; a model of how to audit a popular statistic.
library.limitations: Shows the absence of evidence for 70 per cent, not that change usually succeeds; does not produce an alternative base rate.
library.contested: Challenges claims associated with practitioner literature (see R-kotter-1995-leading); the author revisited the topic in later work.
library.generalizability: The methodological lesson—ask where a number comes from and what its denominator is—applies to every field, including sport.
library.relevance: Trains the reflex of checking the provenance of a statistic before using it to justify urgency or budget.

library.title: The Strength of Weak Ties
library.license: © The University of Chicago. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, journal, volume 78, issue 6, pages 1360–1380 and DOI 10.1086/225469 matched in a BibSonomy record and Wikipedia’s reference list; JSTOR stable URL also reported. Copies circulate on university course pages; library access recommended.

library.summary: Granovetter argues that weak ties — acquaintances rather than close friends — are disproportionately important for moving information and opportunity across social groups, because strong ties tend to connect people who already know each other and share the same information. He links this micro-level property of ties to macro outcomes such as diffusion, mobility and community organization, and supports it with evidence from a study of how professional, technical and managerial workers found jobs.
arguments: Strongly tied people tend to share contacts, so their information is redundant; bridges between groups are almost always weak ties.
Weak ties therefore carry novel information and opportunities across social boundaries.
In the job-search data, people who found jobs through contacts had more often seen those contacts only occasionally or rarely than often.
Communities with few weak ties may struggle to organize collectively.
library.design: Theoretical argument illustrated with data from the author’s survey of people who had recently changed jobs; descriptive, not causal.
library.strengths: Elegant mechanism linking network structure to outcomes; one of the most cited papers in social science; generated decades of testable predictions.
library.limitations: Original evidence is descriptive and limited to one labor market; tie strength was measured crudely by frequency of contact; cannot separate the effect of ties from the characteristics of people who have them.
library.contested: Core claim has been refined rather than overturned: a large randomized test (R-rajkumar-2022-causal) found that moderately weak ties, not the weakest, were most helpful for job mobility.
library.generalizability: Strong for information flow in labor markets and organizations; the importance of weak versus strong ties varies by industry and by what is being transmitted (information versus trust or support).
library.relevance: Explains why the colleague you rarely talk to in another department may be your best source of new information and your best route for spreading a change.

library.summary: A registered replication report in which more than twenty laboratories ran the same preregistered protocol testing whether an initial act of self-control impairs performance on a later self-control task. arguments: A preregistered, multi-site test found an ego-depletion effect near zero.

library.strengths: Preregistration, many labs and large pooled sample remove most of the flexibility that inflated earlier estimates.
library.limitations: Tested one paradigm chosen in consultation with proponents; defenders argued the manipulation was too weak.

library.title: Nobody Ever Gets Credit for Fixing Problems that Never Happened: Creating and Sustaining Process Improvement

library.summary: Using field studies of improvement programs and system-dynamics models, the authors explain why organizations that adopt proven improvement methods so often fail to sustain them. Under pressure to hit targets, people “work harder” instead of “working smarter”; the time diverted from improvement lets capability erode, which raises pressure further—a self-reinforcing capability trap. Managers then tend to blame people rather than the system.
arguments: Improvement competes with production for the same scarce time; short-run pressure systematically favors production.
Working harder produces immediate gains while capability decays slowly and invisibly, so the trap is hard to see from inside.
Managers tend to attribute performance shortfalls to worker effort rather than to the system, reinforcing pressure and control.
Escaping the trap requires deliberately protecting improvement time and accepting a temporary dip in output.
library.design: Comparative field studies of process-improvement initiatives combined with formal system-dynamics modelling.
library.strengths: Mechanism-rich explanation that links individual attribution, incentives and system structure; widely used in operations and healthcare improvement teaching; award-winning article.
library.limitations: Case-based evidence from a limited number of organizations; the models illustrate plausible dynamics rather than estimate effect sizes.
library.generalizability: The mechanism is generic to any setting where improvement work competes with daily output—hospitals, software teams, coaching staffs. Confidence in the mechanism is moderate to high; in any specific magnitude, low.
library.relevance: Explains why departments that are “too busy to improve” stay busy, and why blaming staff for implementation shortfalls is usually the wrong diagnosis.

library.summary: The authors directly replicated Cialdini and colleagues’ 1975 door-in-the-face study, in which a large initial request that is refused increases compliance with a smaller follow-up request. Running the study on a German university campus with 410 people approached by confederates, they found compliance rates similar to the original’s, and results consistent with the reciprocal-concessions explanation. The authors caution that this is one replication of one finding.
arguments: A classic compliance technique replicated in a different country, decades later.
The results support reciprocity norms (reciprocal concessions) as the mechanism.
Older social psychology findings have rarely been the target of direct replication.
library.design: Direct replication with confederates approaching people on a university campus; 410 participants.
library.strengths: Direct, preregistered-style replication of a field finding in a new culture; tests the theoretical mechanism, not only the effect.
library.limitations: One replication of one technique; student-campus setting with one-off requests by strangers, unlike repeated relationships at work.
library.contested: A positive data point in a mixed replication picture for the influence literature reviewed in R-cialdini-2004-social.
library.generalizability: Supports the existence of reciprocity-based concession effects; their size between colleagues who will deal with each other again is unknown.
library.relevance: Shows what a well-replicated influence finding looks like, so you can weigh the rest of the persuasion literature accordingly.

library.summary: A large collaboration repeated 100 studies published in three prominent psychology journals, using high-powered designs and materials from the original authors where possible. Far fewer replications than originals produced statistically significant results, and replication effect sizes were on average about half the original estimates. Social psychology studies replicated less often than cognitive psychology studies.
arguments: Most original studies reported significant results; roughly a third or so of replications did.
Replication effects were, on average, about half the size of the originals.
Original effects that were larger and more strongly significant were more likely to replicate.
Replication rates differed by subfield, with social psychology lower than cognitive psychology.
library.design: Coordinated replication of 100 published studies by many independent teams.
library.strengths: Systematic sampling from journals rather than hand-picked targets; open materials.
library.limitations: One replication per study; some replications differed from originals in population or procedure; what counts as a successful replication is itself debated.
library.contested: Critics argued that differences in samples and procedures depress replication rates; the authors and later many-lab projects responded. The broad conclusion — many published effects are smaller or less reliable than reported — has held.
library.generalizability: Directly relevant to how much weight to give any single classic study cited in management or coaching.
library.relevance: Calibrates your trust in the famous studies that leadership books lean on.

library.title: The Iron Cage Revisited: Institutional Isomorphism and Collective Rationality in Organizational Fields
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

library.summary: DiMaggio and Powell ask why organizations in the same field become so similar. They argue that once a field is established, organizations converge not mainly because similarity is efficient but through institutional isomorphism: coercive pressure from those they depend on and from the state, mimetic copying of organizations seen as successful when uncertainty is high, and normative pressure from professions and their training. Similarity confers legitimacy.
arguments: Organizational fields become homogeneous over time through institutional isomorphism.
Coercive isomorphism stems from dependence and political influence; mimetic isomorphism from uncertainty; normative isomorphism from professionalization.
Practices may be adopted for legitimacy whether or not they improve efficiency.
The paper offers testable hypotheses about which organizations and fields will change fastest.
library.design: Theoretical article with formal hypotheses; tested by a large later literature on the diffusion of practices.
library.strengths: Foundational to neo-institutional theory; explains why “everyone is doing it” is a powerful force independent of results.
library.limitations: Tends to overpredict sameness and underplay agency; isomorphic mechanisms are hard to separate empirically from rational learning.
library.contested: Debate continues on how to distinguish legitimacy-driven adoption from efficiency-driven adoption; resource dependence (R-pfeffer-1978-external) offers a competing explanation of conformity.
library.generalizability: High for public agencies, hospitals, universities, professional services and sports leagues, where professions and peer comparison are strong.
library.relevance: Helps you ask whether a proposed change is being adopted because it works or because peers have it — and how to use legitimacy honestly.

library.summary: Selznick’s study of the Tennessee Valley Authority examines how a federal agency committed to “grass-roots” democratic administration worked through established local institutions and elites. He develops the concept of co-optation — absorbing outside elements into an organization’s leadership or policy-making to avert threats to its stability — and shows how informal co-optation can shift an organization’s actual commitments away from its stated goals.
arguments: Co-optation is a mechanism for gaining support or neutralizing threat by bringing outsiders into the organization’s decision structure.
Formal co-optation shares the appearance of power; informal co-optation shares its substance with powerful local interests.
Co-opted interests can redirect an organization’s programs, so the price of support can be drift from the original mission.
Formal organizations develop informal structures and commitments that constrain leaders.
library.design: Historical-institutional case study of a single federal agency.
library.strengths: Rich case analysis; founding text for the “old” institutionalism and for the study of co-optation; directly relevant to public administration.
library.limitations: Single case; interpretive analysis; the agency’s history is specific to its era.
library.generalizability: The mechanism of co-optation generalizes well to any organization that buys support by sharing control; the specific findings are historical.
library.relevance: Every coalition strategy that gives a resister a seat at the table has the trade-off Selznick documented.

library.summary: Cyert and March replace the profit-maximizing firm of economic theory with a firm that is a coalition of participants whose goals conflict and are negotiated. Goals emerge from bargaining, are stated as aspiration levels, are attended to sequentially, and are held together by side payments and organizational slack; firms search for solutions when performance falls below aspirations and settle for satisfactory rather than optimal outcomes.
arguments: The firm is a coalition of individuals and groups, not a single decision maker with one goal.
Organizational goals are the outcome of bargaining among coalition members and are revised by experience.
Conflict is never fully resolved; it is managed by attending to goals one at a time and by slack resources.
Firms satisfice and search locally, prompted by problems.
library.design: Theoretical book with case studies and computer models of firm decision making.
library.strengths: Founding text of the behavioral theory of organizations; makes politics a normal feature of organizational decision making rather than a pathology.
library.limitations: Abstract about the mechanics of coalition formation; empirical support comes mainly from later research rather than the book itself.
library.generalizability: High: the coalition view fits public agencies, professional service firms and sports organizations as well as industrial firms.
library.relevance: Any change you propose alters a negotiated settlement among coalition members; this book explains why that settlement exists.

library.summary: The standard short statement of self-determination theory. It proposes three basic psychological needs — autonomy, competence and relatedness — and a continuum of motivation from amotivation through externally controlled forms to internalized and intrinsic forms. Social environments that support the three needs are argued to foster internalization, persistence and well-being.
arguments: Motivation varies in kind (autonomous vs. controlled), not only in amount.
Autonomy, competence and relatedness are proposed as universal psychological needs.
Extrinsic motivation can be internalized (identified, integrated regulation) when the context supports the three needs.
library.design: Theoretical review summarizing a research program.
library.strengths: Clear, influential framework with a large empirical literature behind it.
library.limitations: Written by the theory’s founders; summarizes supportive evidence. The universality of the needs and the measurement of the regulation continuum are debated.
library.generalizability: Widely applied to work, education, health and sport; the distinctions are useful for leaders even where effect sizes vary.
library.relevance: Gives you the vocabulary — autonomy, competence, relatedness, internalization — for diagnosing why the same incentive energizes one group and alienates another.

library.summary: A review of compliance and conformity research published mainly between 1997 and 2002. Cialdini and Goldstein organize the literature around the goals that make people susceptible to influence — the desire to be accurate, to affiliate with others, and to maintain a positive self-concept — and argue that influence often operates subtly and outside awareness. The review covers the classic compliance principles, including reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, liking, authority and scarcity.
arguments: Compliance and conformity serve three broad goals: accuracy, affiliation and a positive self-concept.
Classic compliance principles can be understood as shortcuts toward those goals.
Influence often works through subtle, indirect processes outside awareness.
Norms — descriptive (what people do) and injunctive (what people approve) — are powerful influences on behavior.
library.design: Narrative review of the social influence literature.
library.strengths: Authoritative synthesis by the field’s best-known researcher; theoretical organization rather than a list of tricks.
library.limitations: Narrative, not meta-analytic; published before the replication crisis reshaped social psychology, so effect sizes of individual studies were not re-examined.
library.contested: Several individual findings in the influence literature have shown smaller or inconsistent effects in later replications; others, such as the door-in-the-face technique, replicated well (R-genschow-2021-does).
library.generalizability: The principles are general; the size of any technique’s effect in an organizational, repeated-relationship setting is uncertain.
library.relevance: Teaches the mechanisms behind persuasion so you can recognize them — when you use them and when they are used on you.

library.summary: A meta-analysis of studies that used Asch’s line-judgment task, in which a participant faces a unanimous group giving a clearly wrong answer. Conformity was a robust phenomenon, but its size varied: it was larger with larger majorities and in more collectivist cultures, and in U.S. studies it declined over the decades after Asch’s original work.
arguments: Conformity to a unanimous majority is a replicated phenomenon.
Its magnitude depends on group size, the participant’s relationship to the group and culture.
Conformity levels in U.S. samples declined over time, suggesting historical context matters.
library.design: Meta-analysis of Asch-paradigm studies conducted in many countries.
library.strengths: Quantifies a classic finding across time and cultures rather than relying on one iconic study.
library.limitations: Laboratory task with unambiguous stimuli and strangers; conformity in real organizations involves ambiguity, status and consequences.
library.generalizability: The direction (people shift toward unanimous groups) generalizes well; the specific rates do not.
library.relevance: Shows what a robust classic finding looks like when examined carefully: real, but variable and context-dependent.

library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

library.summary: Defines trust as willingness to be vulnerable to another party and separates it from trustworthiness. Perceived trustworthiness rests on ability, benevolence and integrity, moderated by the trustor’s propensity to trust; trust leads to risk-taking in the relationship, whose outcomes update the perceptions.
arguments: Trust is a willingness to accept vulnerability, distinct from its antecedents.
Trustworthiness has three factors: ability, benevolence and integrity.
Trust propensity differs between people and matters most when information is scarce.
Trust produces risk-taking, and outcomes feed back into perceived trustworthiness.
library.strengths: Clear definitions that later empirical work has used widely; distinguishes causes of trust from trust itself.
library.limitations: A conceptual model; its components were tested later by other researchers rather than in this paper.
library.generalizability: High as a diagnostic frame across industries; the relative weight of each factor likely varies by context and relationship stage.
library.relevance: Lets you diagnose which part of trust is broken — competence, care or consistency — instead of treating trust as a mood.

library.title: The ASA’s Statement on p-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 70, issue 2, pages 129–133 and DOI matched in search results (EPA HERO reference record; tandfonline.com / informahealthcare.com DOI page). Free availability is believed but was not separately confirmed.

library.summary: The American Statistical Association’s first formal statement on a matter of statistical practice. It sets out six principles about what p-values can and cannot tell you and explains why the board felt a statement was needed.
arguments: A p-value measures how incompatible the data are with a specified statistical model, not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
Scientific conclusions and business or policy decisions should not rest only on whether a p-value passes a threshold.
Proper inference requires full reporting and transparency; a p-value does not measure the size or importance of an effect.
By itself a p-value is not a good measure of evidence regarding a model or hypothesis.
library.strengths: Consensus statement from a professional body after deliberation among statisticians with differing views; short and readable.
library.limitations: Deliberately says what not to do more than what to do; the accompanying commentaries show statisticians still disagree about replacements (Bayesian methods, estimation, lower thresholds).
library.contested: The principles are broadly accepted; what should replace threshold-based testing remains debated.
library.generalizability: Fully general: applies to any analytics report, vendor study or internal A/B test that reports p-values.
library.relevance: Gives you precise language for challenging analysts and vendors who treat “significant” as “true and important”.

library.title: Structural Holes and Good Ideas
library.license: © The University of Chicago. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, journal, volume 110, issue 2, pages 349–399 and DOI 10.1086/421787 matched in search results (doi listing, Stanford SNAP course reading copy, scilit.com).

library.summary: Burt argues that people whose networks span structural holes — gaps between groups that are not otherwise connected — are more likely to have good ideas, because they see combinations of perspectives that people inside one group do not. Using data on supply-chain managers in a large American electronics company, he reports that managers whose networks spanned holes were more likely to voice ideas, less likely to have them dismissed and more likely to have them judged valuable, and also received more favorable evaluations, compensation and promotion.
arguments: Opinion and behavior are more homogeneous within groups than between them, so brokers across groups see alternatives earlier.
Brokerage across structural holes is associated with ideas that senior managers rate as valuable.
Brokerage is also associated with compensation, positive performance evaluations and promotion.
The value of a good idea depends on being able to move it across groups, not only on generating it.
library.design: Network survey of managers in one company linked to ideas they proposed (rated by senior managers) and to career outcomes; cross-sectional association.
library.strengths: Direct measurement of network structure; outcome measures independent of the respondent (ideas rated by others, compensation records); clear mechanism.
library.limitations: Single firm; observational design cannot rule out that able or ambitious people build brokerage networks (reverse causation); brokerage may carry costs, such as distrust, that the design does not capture.
library.contested: The benefits of brokerage versus closure (dense, trusting networks) remain debated, and appear to depend on culture and task; see R-granovetter-1973-strength for the related weak-ties argument.
library.generalizability: Plausible in knowledge work where combining perspectives matters; less certain in settings that reward loyalty and closure.
library.relevance: Bridging groups — for example across departments, languages or countries — is a structural asset, and also a responsibility.

arguments: The three-step model attributed to Lewin is largely a later reconstruction.

library.relevance: Shows that even the most-taught change model rests on a shaky citation trail—useful discipline for an evidence-minded executive.

library.summary: Based on a multi-year study of Toyota and its suppliers, the authors argue that Toyota’s performance comes not from visible tools such as kanban cards or andon cords but from tacit rules: work is highly specified, connections between people are direct and unambiguous, pathways are simple, and improvements are made by the scientific method at the lowest possible level. The rigid specification of work is what makes flexibility and learning possible.
arguments: Specified work turns every activity into a testable hypothesis, so deviations become visible immediately.
Direct customer–supplier connections and simple pathways make problems traceable to their source.
Improvement is experimentation, done by the people doing the work, under the guidance of a teacher.
Organizations that copy the tools without the underlying rules rarely reproduce the results.
library.design: Multi-year field study of Toyota and supplier plants, reported in a practitioner journal.
library.strengths: Deep field observation; moves the discussion from tools to mechanisms; widely used in healthcare and service operations.
library.limitations: Focused on one exemplary company; rules are inferred by the authors; not a comparative test of performance effects.
library.generalizability: The rules apply most directly to repetitive work but have been adapted widely; transfer depends on management capability, not on tool adoption.
library.relevance: Shows how standardization and learning can reinforce each other—central to any operations or development system you design.

library.title: Transnational Transfer of Strategic Organizational Practices: A Contextual Perspective
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, journal, volume 24(2), pages 308–324 matched across several indexes (scinapse.io, proquest.com, academicnewsletter.sufe.edu.cn); DOI 10.2307/259084 matched on the last.

library.summary: Kostova defines the success of transferring a practice across borders within a multinational as its institutionalization at the receiving unit and proposes a model in which factors at three levels—country (the institutional distance between home and host settings), organization, and individual relationships—shape whether the practice takes hold.
arguments: Transfer success means institutionalization: the practice is both implemented and given meaning and value by the recipients.
The greater the difference between the regulatory, cognitive and normative environments of the two countries, the harder the transfer.
Organizational culture and relationships between units (trust, identification, dependence) also shape transfer.
library.design: Theoretical model with propositions; later tested empirically by the author and colleagues.
library.strengths: Gives precise vocabulary for why a practice can be followed on paper but not believed in.
library.limitations: Propositions rather than tests in this article; measurement of institutional distance is difficult.
library.generalizability: Directly relevant to multi-country organizations, including sports organizations with international academies.
library.relevance: Explains why a development system can be “implemented” at a foreign site while staff privately ignore it—and what to work on instead.

library.title: Transformational and Transactional Leadership: A Meta-Analytic Test of Their Relative Validity
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 89, pages 755–768 and DOI matched in abstract copies (academicnewsletter.sufe.edu.cn, core.ac.uk listings); abstract figures .44 (transformational), .39 (contingent reward), −.37 (laissez-faire) and “626 correlations from 87 sources” matched in the same results.

library.summary: A meta-analysis of the full-range model of leadership. Transformational leadership showed the highest overall validity, but contingent reward, a transactional behavior, was close behind and stronger on several criteria; laissez-faire leadership was negatively related to the criteria.
arguments: Overall validity of .44 for transformational leadership across 626 correlations from 87 sources.
Contingent reward (.39) is nearly as strongly related to outcomes and stronger for some criteria.
Laissez-faire leadership relates negatively (−.37) to the criteria.
library.design: Meta-analysis of 626 correlations from 87 sources relating leadership dimensions to criteria such as follower satisfaction, motivation and leader effectiveness.
library.strengths: Large evidence base; directly compares transformational and transactional behaviors.
library.limitations: Inherits the designs of the primary studies, many of which rate leadership and outcomes from the same source; correlations are not causal estimates.
library.contested: R-vanknippenberg-2013-critical argues that the measures behind these correlations are confounded with the outcomes they predict, so the size of the validities may overstate leader effects.
library.generalizability: Moderate. Associations appear across many settings, but subjective criteria dominate; transfer to objective team performance is less certain.
library.relevance: Gives you the strongest pro-transformational numbers in the field, so you can weigh them against the critique rather than against a slogan.

library.title: When and Why Incentives (Don’t) Work to Modify Behavior
library.license: Free to read from the American Economic Association. Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages, year and DOI matched on econpapers.repec.org and econbiz.de. Open access is from the AEA’s public JEP archive (not separately re-checked this session).

library.summary: A readable review of field and laboratory evidence on when monetary incentives change behavior in the intended direction. The authors argue that incentives have a direct price effect but also change how people interpret a task and what their behavior signals to others and to themselves, so incentives can raise effort in the short run while weakening intrinsic or social motives. They examine education, contributions to public goods, and lifestyle change such as smoking and exercise.
arguments: Incentives have a standard price effect and a psychological effect; the second can work against the first.
Paying for a behavior can change its meaning (from a social obligation to a market exchange), as in the authors’ discussion of fines for late pickup at day-care centers.
Short-run gains under incentives may not persist after incentives are removed, and can crowd out later voluntary engagement.
Design lessons: size, framing, timing and what the incentive signals all matter.
library.design: Narrative review of field experiments and laboratory studies in economics and psychology.
library.strengths: Written for non-specialists; draws on field experiments; balanced about when incentives do work.
library.limitations: A narrative review, not a meta-analysis; selection of studies reflects the authors’ program of research.
library.contested: Crowding-out is well documented in some settings and absent in others; see R-cerasoli-2014-intrinsic for a quantitative synthesis.
library.generalizability: High for public policy, education and health; reasonable for workplaces, where pay is already expected.
library.relevance: The best single entry point into the economics of incentives with behavioral caveats — the vocabulary this week’s exercise and assignment use.

library.title: Examining the Impact of Culture’s Consequences: A Three-Decade, Multilevel, Meta-Analytic Review of Hofstede’s Cultural Value Dimensions
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 95(3), pages 405–439 and DOI 10.1037/a0018938 matched in search results; a post-print is held in the University of Calgary repository (prism.ucalgary.ca), which notes it is not the copy of record.

library.summary: A meta-analysis of 598 studies covering more than 200,000 individuals tests how well Hofstede’s original four cultural value dimensions predict organizational outcomes. Relationships are modest on average (an overall absolute weighted correlation of about .18 at the individual level), stronger for emotions and attitudes than for behaviors and job performance, and stronger in culturally “tighter” countries.
arguments: Cultural values have real but modest predictive power for work outcomes.
They predict job performance, absenteeism and turnover less well than personality and demographics do, but predict commitment and citizenship behavior better.
Effects are strongest for emotions, then attitudes, then behaviors, and weakest for performance.
Context matters: effects are larger in tighter societies with stronger norms.
library.design: Multilevel meta-analysis of 598 studies (more than 200,000 individuals).
library.strengths: Very large evidence base; tests the dimensions against outcomes rather than assuming them; compares with other predictors.
library.limitations: Depends on the quality of primary studies, most of which are correlational; aggregate effects say little about any one person or workplace.
library.contested: Hofstede’s framework itself is criticized on conceptual and methodological grounds (see R-mcsweeney-2002-hofstedes).
library.generalizability: Supports using cultural dimensions as weak priors about groups, not as predictions about individuals or as the main design input for a rollout.
library.relevance: Lets you use cultural frameworks with calibrated confidence instead of either dismissing or over-applying them.

c-compliance-principles.name: Compliance principles and their replication record

glossary.definition: The tendency of observers to explain others’ behavior by their dispositions while underweighting the situational pressures acting on them; also called correspondence bias.
Changing one’s judgments or behavior to match those of a group. In Asch-type tasks it is robust but varies with majority size, culture and era.
Repeating a study’s procedure as closely as possible with new participants to test whether the original result is reliable.
A replication whose protocol and analysis are fixed and reviewed in advance, often run across many laboratories, so that results are published regardless of outcome.
The claim that self-control draws on a limited resource used up by earlier acts of self-control; a large preregistered multi-lab test found an effect near zero.
A theory of motivation distinguishing autonomous from controlled motivation and proposing that support for autonomy, competence and relatedness fosters the former.
Doing an activity because it is interesting or satisfying in itself, rather than for a separable outcome such as pay or approval.
The process by which an externally prompted behavior comes to be valued and self-endorsed (identified or integrated regulation), making it autonomous though not intrinsically enjoyable.
When an external incentive weakens an existing intrinsic or social motive, for example by turning a moral obligation into a purchasable service; the reverse is crowding in.
The difficulty that arises when a principal delegates work to an agent whose actions cannot be fully observed and whose interests differ, creating hidden action and hidden information.

When an agent divides effort among tasks that differ in measurability, strong incentives on the measured tasks divert effort from the unmeasured ones; weaker incentives or job redesign may be optimal.
The heuristic that a measure loses its value as an indicator once it becomes a target, because people find cheaper ways to move the measure than the goal. Related to Campbell’s law.
How incentive pay changes with the measure — linear, threshold, capped, relative or deferred — which determines where marginal incentives are strongest and which gaming strategies pay.
Responding to kind actions with kindness and to unkind actions with retaliation, even at personal cost; it helps enforce incomplete contracts and norms.
Contributing to shared efforts when others do and withdrawing when others free ride, which makes group cooperation fragile without sanctions.
A shared expectation about what people do and ought to do, enforced informally through approval and disapproval.
The benchmark — prior outcome, peer outcome or expectation — against which an outcome is judged as a gain, a loss, fair or unfair.
A shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks such as asking questions or admitting errors; associated with learning and performance, mostly in correlational studies.
The tendency of cases selected for extreme values on a noisy measure to be closer to the average when measured again, with or without any intervention.
The consistency of a measure: the share of its variation that reflects stable differences rather than noise. Low reliability attenuates observed effects.
The degree to which a measure captures the construct it claims to measure, and supports the inferences drawn from it.
A range produced by a procedure that captures the true value in a stated share of repeated samples (for example 95%); read as the effect sizes reasonably compatible with the data.
The probability of data at least as extreme as those observed if a specified model, usually of no effect, were true. Not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
The probability that a study detects a true effect of a given size at its significance threshold; it rises with sample size, effect size and measurement precision.

glossary.term: Type M and type S errors
glossary.definition: A type M error is an exaggerated estimate of an effect’s magnitude; a type S error is an estimate with the wrong sign. Both are common among significant results from low-powered studies.
The many analytic choices (outcomes, samples, covariates, stopping rules) that, when made after seeing the data, inflate false positives.
The selective publication or presentation of results depending on their significance or direction, which distorts the visible body of evidence.
A time-stamped plan specifying hypotheses, outcomes and analyses before data are collected or seen.
A publication format in which a journal reviews and accepts a study’s question and design before results exist, so publication does not depend on the outcome.
The outcome that would have occurred for the same units without the treatment; every causal effect compares an observed outcome with a counterfactual.
A variable that influences both the treatment and the outcome, creating an association that is not the treatment’s effect.
A variable caused by both the treatment and the outcome (or their causes); selecting on or adjusting for it creates a spurious association.
A design that compares the change over time in a treated group with the change in an untreated group, assuming their trends would otherwise have been parallel.
A design that compares units just above and just below a cutoff that determines treatment.
A factor that changes the likelihood of treatment but affects the outcome only through the treatment, such as a lottery for program slots.
Whether a result obtained in one population, setting and time holds in others.
The principle that an indicator used as a target or for high-stakes decisions tends to be gamed and to lose its value as a measure.
A statistical synthesis that pools estimates from several studies, weighted by precision, and examines how much they vary (heterogeneity).
The tendency of observers to explain organizational outcomes by pointing to leaders, strongest after extreme outcomes.
An observer’s inference that a person is or is not an effective leader, often drawn from outcomes and impressions rather than observed behavior.
A family of leader behaviors — articulating a vision, modeling values, stimulating and supporting followers — claimed to raise performance beyond expectations; its measurement is disputed.
A transactional leader behavior: agreeing on goals with people and recognizing or rewarding them when the goals are met.
The absence of leadership: avoiding decisions, being unavailable and not responding to problems; consistently associated with worse outcomes.
A perspective holding that leaders form relationships of different quality with different followers, and that relationship quality relates to outcomes.
A willingness to be vulnerable to another party based on the expectation that they will act in a way important to you, without your being able to monitor or control them.
The perceived characteristics that lead someone to trust another: ability, benevolence and integrity.
A shared belief among team members that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking, such as admitting errors or raising concerns.
The theory that feedback works by directing attention, and that it helps less or harms when it draws attention from the task toward the self.
A practitioner technique of asking for suggestions about future behavior instead of evaluating past behavior; plausible but thinly researched.
The explicit degree of decision authority given to a person for a type of decision, from being told what to do to full ownership.
A practitioner writing convention, from U.S. military usage, that places the conclusion or request in the opening sentences.
A practitioner structure, associated with Barbara Minto’s consulting writing, that places a governing idea first, supported by grouped arguments and then evidence.
Working out an audience’s decision rights, prior beliefs, accountability and vocabulary before deciding what to say and in what order.
A popular term for the impression that a person has the judgment and composure of a senior leader; mostly described in practitioner writing rather than validated research.
The capacity to affect what others do, including when they would prefer otherwise; relational and situational rather than a fixed possession.
Power accepted as legitimate because of a position or rule; the right to direct, recognized by those who are directed.
French and Raven’s typology of the reasons a target complies: reward, coercive, legitimate, referent and expert power, with informational power added later by Raven.
The principle that A’s power over B equals B’s dependence on A, which grows with the importance of what A controls, A’s discretion over it, and B’s lack of alternatives.

Pfeffer and Salancik’s theory that organizations are shaped by dependence on actors who control critical resources, and act to manage that dependence through co-optation, alliances, mergers and diversification.
A relationship of low frequency or intimacy, such as an acquaintance; per Granovetter, the kind of tie that usually bridges groups and carries new information.
A gap between two groups that are not otherwise connected and hold different information; spanning it gives a broker earlier, more diverse information.
A person whose ties connect otherwise disconnected people or groups; gains information and control benefits and may face distrust or overload.
A dense network in which most members are connected to one another; it supports trust and norm enforcement but tends to circulate redundant information.
The informal network showing whom people rely on for technical help and information; distinct from the trust network.
The informal network showing with whom people share sensitive information and whom they back in a crisis; decisive for whether a change is believed.
The subset of organizational members whose agreement actually determines major decisions; not necessarily the top of the formal chart.
In the behavioral theory of the firm, the inducements — budget, status, autonomy, policy commitments — that keep coalition members committed to the organization.
Resources beyond what is strictly needed for current operations, which allow an organization to satisfy several coalition members at once and to absorb conflict.
The process by which organizations in a field become similar through coercive, mimetic and normative pressures rather than only through efficiency.
The perception that an organization or practice is appropriate and proper within a system of norms and beliefs; it helps secure resources and support.
Absorbing outside or opposing elements into an organization’s leadership or decision structure to avert threats; Selznick showed it can shift the organization’s actual commitments.
Efforts by people below the top to direct senior leaders’ attention to particular issues and shape how they are understood, through packaging and process.
A behavior used to change another person’s attitudes or actions, such as rational persuasion, consultation, exchange, legitimating or pressure.
Commitment is inward agreement and effort to make a request succeed; compliance is doing what is asked without belief, often minimally.
The difference between an organization’s stated strategic choices and the pattern of work, resource allocation and attention that actually follows.
A self-reinforcing loop in which pressure to meet targets diverts time from improvement, capability erodes, performance falls further, and leaders blame people rather than the system.
The recurring cadence of reviews—daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly—through which an organization notices deviations and makes decisions.
In Weiner’s definition, a shared psychological state combining change commitment and change efficacy among the members of an organization.
Members’ shared resolve to implement a change; strongest when they value it, weaker when they comply from obligation or lack of choice.
Members’ shared belief that they can carry out a change, based on their appraisal of task demands, resources and circumstances.
For a stable system over the long run, average work-in-process equals throughput multiplied by average time in the system (L = λW).
The number of items started but not yet finished in a system, such as open cases, contracts or patients.
The step in a process with the least capacity relative to demand; it sets the pace of the whole system.
The share of available time a resource is busy; with variability, waiting time rises steeply as utilization approaches 100 per cent.
A precise specification of how a task is done and what result it should produce, used as a hypothesis so that deviations become visible and can be investigated.
A measure of a behavior or condition believed to drive a later outcome, observable quickly enough to act on; its causal link should be tested.
A measure of the outcome an organization ultimately cares about, which arrives late and reflects many causes.
The degree of difference between two countries’ regulatory, cognitive and normative environments, which makes transferring organizational practices harder.
A practice carried out formally—forms filed, meetings held—while the people involved do not value it, so it produces little of its intended effect.
The distinction between the elements of an intervention believed to produce its benefit, which should be kept, and elements that can be tailored to each setting.

The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research: a structured set of constructs in five domains—intervention, outer setting, inner setting, individuals and process—for diagnosing implementation.
The error of inferring individual characteristics or relationships from group-level averages, such as assuming a person holds their country’s average values.
